shard.title: South Asia: the Company, the Raj, the princely states, Ceylon, Burma and the Himalayan kingdoms
shard.author: south-asia historian agent
shard.note: Thirty territories and thirty-six events, 1600 to 1971. Provinces and princely states are nested inside british-india, which is why their unit claims overlap it. Where the drawn geometry differs from the historical extent, the difference is stated in that territory contested note.

territories.name: British India
territories.formalName: The Indian Empire: British India and the princely states

namesOverTime.name: The Company's settlements
namesOverTime.note: Before 1765 there was no 'British India': there were fortified trading posts held on Mughal sufferance.

namesOverTime.name: The Raj
namesOverTime.note: Raj simply means 'rule'. It came into English as shorthand for the Crown period after 1858.

from.note: A pre-existing Persian and Hindustani name for the northern plains, used long before and long after the English arrived; it has no single fixed boundary.

modernSuccessors.name: India
modernSuccessors.note: A republic since 26 January 1950. Sikkim stayed a protected state until 1975.

modernSuccessors.name: Pakistan
modernSuccessors.note: Pakistan in 1947 had two wings 1,600 km apart with India between them. The eastern wing left in 1971.

modernSuccessors.name: Bangladesh
modernSuccessors.note: East Bengal in 1947, East Pakistan from 1955, independent after the war of 1971.

modernSuccessors.name: Myanmar
modernSuccessors.note: Governed as a province of British India until 1 April 1937, then as a separate colony.

modernSuccessors.name: Yemen
modernSuccessors.note: Aden was run from Bombay for 98 years. The empire's filing system, not its geography, decided that.

geoCoverage.label: Coastal factories only
geoCoverage.change: Walled warehouses at Masulipatam, Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, licensed by Mughal or Nayak rulers. Draw these as dots, not provinces: the Company held perhaps a few hundred acres.

geoCoverage.label: The diwani of Bengal
geoCoverage.change: The Treaty of Allahabad made a shareholder company the tax collector of roughly 20 million people. Orissa is hatched: the Marathas held most of it until 1803.

geoCoverage.label: Malabar taken from Mysore
geoCoverage.change: Beaten in the Third Anglo-Mysore War, Tipu Sultan gave up half his kingdom, including the Malabar pepper coast, and handed over two of his sons as hostages.

geoCoverage.label: Hyderabad signs the first subsidiary alliance
geoCoverage.change: The Nizam of Hyderabad agreed to disband his French-trained army, pay for Company troops instead, and hand his foreign policy to Calcutta. Wellesley then used the model on every state he could reach.

geoCoverage.label: Mysore destroyed
geoCoverage.change: Tipu Sultan was killed defending Seringapatam. The Company kept the coast and the passes, put a five-year-old Wodeyar prince on a shrunken throne, and took the Carnatic outright in 1801.

geoCoverage.label: Delhi and the Ganges plain
geoCoverage.change: Lake beat the Marathas at Delhi and Laswari; the blind Mughal emperor Shah Alam II passed under Company protection, a pensioner in his own palace.

geoCoverage.label: Maratha power ended; the Rajput states brought in
geoCoverage.change: The Peshwa surrendered and his office was abolished. Between 1817 and 1818 the Rajput and central Indian courts signed subsidiary treaties, and two fifths of the subcontinent became princely states rather than provinces.

geoCoverage.label: Assam, Arakan and Tenasserim
geoCoverage.change: The Treaty of Yandabo ended the First Anglo-Burmese War: Burma gave up Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim and paid an indemnity of a million pounds. The hill country was claimed on paper decades before anyone administered it.

geoCoverage.label: Aden, on the far side of the ocean
geoCoverage.change: Aden was stormed by a Bombay Marine expedition to make a coaling station for steamers, and was governed from Bombay for the next 98 years. India's empire had an empire.

geoCoverage.label: Sindh
geoCoverage.change: Charles Napier picked a quarrel with the Talpur amirs, destroyed them at Miani, and annexed Sindh against his own government's instructions.

geoCoverage.label: Kashmir sold to a Dogra raja
geoCoverage.change: After the First Anglo-Sikh War the Company sold Kashmir and its people to Gulab Singh of Jammu for 7.5 million rupees, creating the state whose ownership India and Pakistan still dispute.

geoCoverage.label: The Punjab annexed
geoCoverage.change: Two wars ended the Sikh empire, the last army in the subcontinent that could beat the Company in the field. Its maharaja Duleep Singh, ten years old, was deposed and the Koh-i-Noor sent to Queen Victoria.

geoCoverage.label: Pegu; then Awadh in 1856
geoCoverage.change: Dalhousie annexed Lower Burma after a quarrel over harbour dues, and in February 1856 annexed Awadh, whose king he called incompetent. A third of the Bengal army came from Awadh, and they noticed.

geoCoverage.label: A penal colony in the Andamans
geoCoverage.change: Port Blair was founded in March 1858 to hold prisoners taken in the rebellion. The islands' Great Andamanese population fell by roughly nine tenths within fifty years, mostly from introduced disease.

geoCoverage.label: Balochistan and the road to Kandahar
geoCoverage.change: Robert Sandeman's treaties with the Khan of Kalat and the Baloch sardars put Quetta under British garrison and made Balochistan a buffer aimed at Russia, not a province anyone wanted to govern.

geoCoverage.label: Upper Burma swallowed
geoCoverage.change: Three weeks after taking Mandalay, Britain abolished the Burmese monarchy by proclamation and attached the kingdom to India as a province. Guerrilla resistance in the countryside took five more years to break.

geoCoverage.label: Greatest extent
geoCoverage.change: The Anglo-Chinese Convention made Sikkim a British protectorate and opened the road to Tibet. From here the Indian Empire only shrank: a fifth of the world's people under one Viceroy.

geoCoverage.label: After Burma and Aden are detached
geoCoverage.change: The Government of India Act 1935 made Burma and Aden separate colonies on 1 April 1937. They stayed British; they stopped being India. Burmese nationalists had asked to be separated and then suspected a trick.

acquisitions.how: Elizabeth I gave 218 London merchants a fifteen-year monopoly of English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope. The charter granted no land, no soldiers and no authority over anybody in Asia.

counterparties.name: Other English merchants
counterparties.lost: The legal right to trade east of the Cape. The charter was a weapon against rival Englishmen, not a claim on India.

instrument.name: Royal charter to the Governor and Company of Merchants of London trading into the East Indies

people.name: Elizabeth I
people.role: granted the charter to raise English trade against Portuguese and Dutch competition

people.name: Thomas Smythe
people.role: first governor of the Company

acquisitions.how: After Thomas Best beat a Portuguese squadron off Swally, the emperor Jahangir licensed the Company to keep a warehouse at Surat and pay Mughal customs like any other merchant.

counterparties.name: Mughal Empire
counterparties.lost: Nothing yet. Jahangir ruled perhaps 100 million people and treated the English as a minor trading nuisance worth taxing.
counterparties.note: The asymmetry is the point. In 1612 the Company was by far the weaker party, and stayed weaker for 150 years.

people.name: Jahangir
people.role: Mughal emperor who licensed the factory

people.name: Thomas Roe
people.role: James I's ambassador at the Mughal court, 1615-19, who negotiated trading rights and was kept waiting

contested.note: Sources date the Surat farman to 1612, 1613 or 1618 depending on which document is counted as the grant. The atlas uses 1612, the year the factory was established.

acquisitions.how: Francis Day leased a three-mile strip of surf-beaten sand from the Nayak of Kalahasti, on which the Company built Fort St George and the town that became Madras.

counterparties.name: Damarla Venkatadri Nayak of Vandavasi and Poonamallee
counterparties.lost: The rent from a stretch of coast, and eventually the coast itself. The grant was made in the hope that European trade would enrich his ports.

instrument.name: Grant of the Nayak of Kalahasti to the East India Company
instrument.note: The Company paid an annual rent and took half the customs. Contemporary copies differ; the date 22 August 1639 comes from the Company's own record.

people.name: Francis Day
people.role: Company agent who chose the site, allegedly to be near his mistress at Portuguese Sao Tome

people.name: Andrew Cogan
people.role: agent at Masulipatam who backed the settlement

contested.note: The identity of the granting Nayak and the exact terms are disputed; the story that Day chose Madras for personal reasons comes from a later Company tradition and may be a joke that hardened into a fact.

acquisitions.how: Portugal handed Bombay's seven islands to Charles II as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry; the Crown could not make them pay and rented them to the Company in 1668 for ten pounds a year.

counterparties.name: Kingdom of Portugal
counterparties.lost: A malarial harbour it valued little, given away to buy an English alliance against Spain and the Dutch.

counterparties.name: The Koli fisher communities of the islands
counterparties.lost: Their islands changed owner twice in seven years without anyone asking them. Their villages are still named on the modern map of Mumbai.

instrument.name: Anglo-Portuguese marriage treaty of 1661
instrument.note: The dowry also included Tangier and a payment of two million Portuguese crowns. Portuguese officials in India delayed the actual handover until February 1665.

people.name: Catherine of Braganza
people.role: Portuguese princess whose marriage contract transferred Bombay

people.name: Gerald Aungier
people.role: Governor 1669-77 who built the docks, courts and fortifications that made Bombay a city

acquisitions.how: Job Charnock landed for the third time at the village of Sutanuti on the Hooghly, three years after the Company had lost a war with the emperor Aurangzeb and had to apologise to get its trade back.

counterparties.name: Mughal Empire and the villagers of Sutanuti, Kalikata and Govindapur
counterparties.lost: Nothing in 1690. The Company paid 1,300 rupees for the rent rights of the three villages in 1698, with Mughal permission.

people.name: Job Charnock
people.role: Company agent who founded the settlement

people.name: Aurangzeb
people.role: Mughal emperor who defeated the Company in 1686-90 and then let it return as a taxpayer

acquisitions.resistance: In 1686 the Company declared war on the Mughal empire, lost every engagement, was expelled from Bengal, and was readmitted only after paying a fine of 150,000 rupees.

contested.note: In 2003 the Calcutta High Court ruled that the city had no single founder and no 1690 birthday, on the evidence that the villages long predated Charnock. Both statements are true: the settlement dates from 1690, the place does not.

acquisitions.how: After winning at Plassey in 1757 by buying the Nawab's commander, and at Buxar in 1764 by beating three Indian armies at once, Robert Clive made the Mughal emperor sign over the right to tax Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to a company of London shareholders.

counterparties.name: Shah Alam II, Mughal emperor
counterparties.lost: The revenue of the richest province of his empire, and with it any means of paying an army. He was given 2.6 million rupees a year and a palace.

counterparties.name: The Nawabs of Bengal
counterparties.lost: Real power. Mir Jafar and his successors kept the title, the palace and a pension, and became salaried figureheads.

counterparties.name: The peasants and weavers of Bengal
counterparties.lost: Any court to appeal to. Revenue demands were now set by men whose shareholders lived 8,000 km away and who had no reason to leave a reserve for a bad harvest.

people.name: Robert Clive
people.role: Company commander and negotiator; took a personal fortune out of Bengal and was investigated for it by Parliament

people.name: Shah Alam II
people.role: Mughal emperor who signed away the diwani

people.name: Mir Qasim
people.role: Nawab who tried to govern independently, fought the Company and lost at Buxar

people.name: Mir Madan
people.role: Bengali artillery commander who fought and died at Plassey while his colleague Mir Jafar stood still

people.name: Jagat Seth Mahtab Rai
people.role: head of the banking house that financed the plot against Siraj-ud-Daula

cost.note: The Bengal famine of 1770 killed between roughly one and ten million people, often given as up to a third of the province, while the Company went on collecting revenue and its servants traded in grain. There was no census; contemporary estimates were political documents.

warrant.author: Contemporary Company estimates, against later reconstructions
warrant.work: The range of estimates for the Bengal famine of 1769–70
warrant.supports: The Bengal famine of 1770 killed between roughly one and ten million people, often given as up to a third of the province, while the Company went on collecting revenue and its servants traded in grain. There was no census; contemporary estimates were political documents.
warrant.check: The contemporary figures are in the Company’s Bengal correspondence, India Office Records, British Library. There was no census to check them against.
warrant.note: The record says it plainly: contemporary estimates were political documents. "A third of the province" was an assertion made by men with an interest in its size.

acquisitions.resistance: Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Awadh and the Mughal emperor combined their armies and were beaten at Buxar on 22 October 1764, the battle that mattered more than Plassey.

evidence.author: William Dalrymple
evidence.work: The Anarchy: The Relentless Rise of the East India Company
evidence.supports: Plassey, Buxar, the bankers' role and the seizure of the diwani.

acquisitions.how: Cornwallis besieged Seringapatam and forced Tipu Sultan to give up half his kingdom, pay 33 million rupees, and hand over two of his young sons as hostages until the money came.

counterparties.name: Sultanate of Mysore under Tipu Sultan
counterparties.lost: Malabar, Coorg, the Baramahal and Dindigul: the pepper coast and the eastern passes, taken by the Company, the Nizam and the Marathas together.

people.name: Tipu Sultan
people.role: ruler of Mysore, who modernised his army and navy and fought four wars against the Company

people.name: Charles Cornwallis
people.role: Governor-General who commanded the siege, eleven years after surrendering at Yorktown

acquisitions.how: Richard Wellesley made the Nizam disband his French-officered battalions, accept Company troops he had to pay for, and give up the right to deal with any other power without British consent.

counterparties.name: Nizam of Hyderabad, Asaf Jah II
counterparties.lost: His army, his foreign policy and, through the subsidy, control of his own revenue. He kept his throne, his titles and his internal power.

people.name: Richard Wellesley
people.role: Governor-General 1798-1805 who built the subsidiary alliance system

people.name: Asaf Jah II, Nizam Ali Khan
people.role: ruler of Hyderabad who signed

acquisitions.how: Company and Hyderabad troops stormed Seringapatam and killed Tipu Sultan at the breach; his kingdom was carved up and a five-year-old Wodeyar prince installed over what was left.

counterparties.name: Sultanate of Mysore
counterparties.lost: Its independence and its dynasty. Tipu's family were deported to Vellore; his library, throne and tiger automaton were shipped to Britain.

people.name: Tipu Sultan
people.role: killed defending the breach; the last Indian ruler to die fighting the Company in the field

people.name: Arthur Wellesley
people.role: commanded a division at the siege and governed Seringapatam afterwards; later Duke of Wellington

cost.note: Roughly 6,000 to 9,000 of Tipu's soldiers were killed in the assault and about 1,400 attackers, on British siege returns. Civilian deaths in the sacked city were not counted.

warrant.author: The British siege train at Seringapatam, in its own returns
warrant.work: British siege returns of the fourth Anglo-Mysore war
warrant.supports: Roughly 6,000 to 9,000 of Tipu's soldiers were killed in the assault and about 1,400 attackers, on British siege returns. Civilian deaths in the sacked city were not counted.
warrant.check: East India Company and Government of India military returns are in the India Office Records at the British Library (IOR series) and in the WO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: The attackers’ dead were counted to the man; Tipu’s were estimated, and the civilians killed in the sack of the city were not counted at all.

acquisitions.resistance: Tipu had sought alliances with France, the Ottomans and Afghanistan, and had beaten the Company badly in 1780-84. He was killed with a musket in his hands, not in flight.

acquisitions.how: After Assaye and Laswari, Scindia ceded Delhi, the Ganges-Jumna Doab, Broach and Cuttack; the blind Mughal emperor passed from Maratha protection to Company protection without leaving his palace.

counterparties.name: Daulat Rao Scindia of Gwalior
counterparties.lost: The Doab, Delhi, Ahmednagar and the guardianship of the Mughal emperor, which was the last shred of legitimacy in northern India.

counterparties.name: Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur
counterparties.lost: Cuttack and Orissa, which joined Bengal to Madras along the coast for the first time.

people.name: Gerard Lake
people.role: commander who took Delhi and Agra

people.name: Yashwantrao Holkar
people.role: Maratha ruler of Indore who fought on after 1803 and forced a negotiated peace in 1806

acquisitions.how: Peshwa Baji Rao II surrendered to John Malcolm, his office was abolished and his lands taken; in the same eighteen months the Rajput and central Indian courts signed subsidiary treaties rather than be next.

counterparties.name: The Maratha confederacy
counterparties.lost: The Peshwa's office, the Deccan heartland and the last coalition capable of contesting the subcontinent. Baji Rao II was pensioned off to Bithur near Kanpur.

counterparties.name: The Pindari bands
counterparties.lost: Their livelihood and, for many, their lives: the campaign that broke them was fought by 120,000 troops, the largest British force yet assembled in India.

people.name: Baji Rao II
people.role: last Peshwa; his adopted son Nana Sahib led the rising at Kanpur in 1857

people.name: Francis Rawdon-Hastings
people.role: Governor-General who ordered the campaign

people.name: John Malcolm
people.role: negotiated the treaties that turned defeated states into princely states

acquisitions.how: British and Indian troops had already occupied Arakan, Tenasserim and Assam and held Rangoon for a year when the Konbaung court signed at Yandabo, giving up all four and an indemnity of one million pounds sterling.

counterparties.name: Konbaung kingdom of Burma
counterparties.lost: Its western conquests and its western coast, plus an indemnity that crippled its finances for a generation.

counterparties.name: The Ahom kingdom and the Manipuri and hill polities of the north-east
counterparties.lost: They were transferred between two empires without being consulted. The Ahom dynasty, which had ruled Assam for 600 years, was pensioned off by 1838.

cost.money: About 13 million pounds, the most expensive war the Company had yet fought; it nearly bankrupted the Bengal treasury.
cost.note: Most British and Indian deaths were from disease rather than fighting. Burmese losses were never counted.

warrant.author: The Company army, in its own casualty and medical returns
warrant.work: British and Company returns of the first Anglo-Burmese war
warrant.supports: Most British and Indian deaths were from disease rather than fighting. Burmese losses were never counted.
warrant.check: East India Company and Government of India returns are in the India Office Records at the British Library (IOR series) and in the WO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: Most of the British and Indian dead were killed by disease. Burmese losses were never counted.

acquisitions.how: A Bombay Marine expedition under Stafford Haines bombarded and stormed Aden, using a plundered shipwreck as the pretext, to secure coal for steamers on the route to Suez.

counterparties.name: Sultanate of Lahej
counterparties.lost: Its port and its customs revenue. The sultan was offered a stipend and refused it for years.

acquisitions.how: Charles Napier imposed a treaty the Talpur amirs could not accept, destroyed their army at Miani, and annexed Sindh; the Company's own directors called the war unjustified and kept the province.

counterparties.name: The Talpur amirs of Sindh
counterparties.lost: Their state, their treasury and their hunting reserves along the Indus. The amirs were deported to Calcutta.

people.name: Charles Napier
people.role: general who provoked and won the war, and privately wrote that it was a piece of rascality

people.name: Mir Nasir Khan Talpur
people.role: amir of Hyderabad in Sindh, defeated at Miani and exiled

acquisitions.how: The Company sold Kashmir, Jammu, Ladakh and their people to Gulab Singh of Jammu for 7.5 million rupees, having taken the country from the defeated Sikh state a week earlier.

counterparties.name: The Sikh empire
counterparties.lost: Kashmir and the Jalandhar Doab, and an indemnity of 15 million rupees it could not pay, which is why Kashmir was sold.

counterparties.name: The people of Kashmir
counterparties.lost: They were transferred by bill of sale to a Dogra ruler of a different religion from most of them, a grievance that runs straight into 1947.

people.name: Gulab Singh
people.role: Dogra general who bought the state and founded its dynasty

people.name: Henry Hardinge
people.role: Governor-General who preferred a client buffer state to another province to garrison

acquisitions.how: After two wars and the bloodiest battles the Company ever fought in India, the Sikh empire was annexed, its ten-year-old maharaja Duleep Singh deposed and later shipped to England, and the Koh-i-Noor taken as indemnity.

counterparties.name: The Sikh empire of Ranjit Singh's successors
counterparties.lost: Independence, the treasury and the last army in the subcontinent that could beat the Company in open battle. Chillianwala in January 1849 was close to a British defeat.

counterparties.name: Duleep Singh
counterparties.lost: His throne at ten - he was born on 6 September 1838 and signed the terms on 29 March 1849; he was then separated from his mother, converted to Christianity and settled in Norfolk on a pension.

people.name: Duleep Singh
people.role: last maharaja of the Sikh empire, deposed and exiled

people.name: Rani Jind Kaur
people.role: his mother and regent, imprisoned and exiled for resisting the annexation

people.name: James Broun-Ramsay, Lord Dalhousie
people.role: Governor-General who ordered the annexation

acquisitions.how: A dispute over harbour dues charged to two British ship captains in Rangoon ended with Dalhousie annexing the whole province of Pegu by proclamation, without a treaty and without asking London.

counterparties.name: Konbaung kingdom of Burma
counterparties.lost: Its coastline and its only ports. Burma was now landlocked and its king had no treaty to sign, because none was offered.

acquisitions.how: Two hundred prisoners taken in the rebellion were landed at Port Blair to clear jungle for the penal settlement that became the Cellular Jail, on islands whose people had kept Europeans out for a century.

counterparties.name: The Great Andamanese, Jarawa, Onge and Sentinelese peoples
counterparties.lost: Their islands and, for the Great Andamanese, most of their population: roughly 5,000 people in 1858 and 19 by 1961, mainly through measles, syphilis and influenza.

people.name: James Pattison Walker
people.role: surgeon who commanded the first convict party

acquisitions.resistance: The Andamanese attacked the settlement at Aberdeen in May 1859; the Jarawa and the Sentinelese refused contact altogether and the Sentinelese still do.

contested.note: Pre-contact Andamanese population figures are estimates from colonial censuses that never counted the interior; the collapse is undisputed, its exact scale is not.

acquisitions.how: Robert Sandeman settled the Baloch sardars with subsidies and treaties, put a garrison in Quetta and made the Khan of Kalat a protected ruler, to hold the passes against Russia.

counterparties.name: Khanate of Kalat
counterparties.lost: Control of its own foreign relations and of Quetta, which was leased to Britain and never returned.

counterparties.name: The Baloch and Brahui sardars
counterparties.lost: Independence of action, in exchange for subsidies and British recognition of their authority over their own people.

instrument.name: Treaty of Jacobabad with the Khan of Kalat

people.name: Robert Sandeman
people.role: agent whose system of paying Baloch sardars was copied across the frontier

people.name: Khudadad Khan
people.role: Khan of Kalat who signed away his external sovereignty

contested.note: Whether Kalat was ever legally part of British India or only a protected state outside it is disputed, and the argument matters: Kalat used it in 1947 to claim independence.

acquisitions.how: Three weeks after taking Mandalay in an eleven-day war, Britain abolished the Burmese monarchy by proclamation, exiled King Thibaw to India, and attached his kingdom to British India as a province.

counterparties.name: Konbaung kingdom of Burma
counterparties.lost: Its monarchy and its existence as a state. King Thibaw and Queen Supayalat died in exile at Ratnagiri.

counterparties.name: The Shan, Kachin, Chin and Karenni polities
counterparties.lost: They were declared British by the same proclamation and then subdued one by one over the following decade.

acquisitions.resistance: Guerrilla war continued until about 1890 and needed 30,000 troops to suppress; British reports called the fighters dacoits, which let them be hanged rather than treated as prisoners of war.

acquisitions.how: Britain and China signed a convention over Sikkim's head recognising a British protectorate and fixing the Tibetan border; the Chogyal, who had tried to keep both out, was already under detention.

counterparties.name: The Chogyal of Sikkim, Thutob Namgyal
counterparties.lost: His foreign policy, his freedom of movement and his trade with Tibet. He was held at Kurseong and Darjeeling for years.

counterparties.name: Qing China
counterparties.lost: Its claim to suzerainty over Sikkim, signed away without Sikkimese participation.

statusPeriods.label: Company factories under Mughal licence
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Company rented walled warehouses, paid Mughal customs and could be thrown out at any time; when it fought Aurangzeb in 1686 it lost, paid a fine and apologised on its knees.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Court of Directors, Leadenhall Street, London
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody in India voted for anything. In London the Company's shareholders elected its directors, and a vote cost 500 pounds of stock.

statusPeriods.label: Company rule from Calcutta
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A private company with shareholders in London collected the land tax of northern India through Indian revenue officials and enforced it with an army that reached about 280,000 men at its peak on the eve of 1857, most of them Indian.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Calcutta, under the Court of Directors and, after 1784, a government Board of Control in London
statusPeriods.franchise: No Indian could vote. The Governor-General's executive council had no Indian member until S. P. Sinha in 1909. Indians sat on the larger legislative council from the Indian Councils Act of 1861 — Benares, Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao in 1862 — but they were nominated, not elected.
statusPeriods.note: Parliament tightened its grip in stages: the Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, and the charter renewals of 1813, 1833 and 1853, which stripped the Company of its trade and left it governing.

statusPeriods.label: The Raj: direct Crown rule
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Viceroy in Calcutta, then New Delhi, answered to a Secretary of State in the British Cabinet; about a thousand covenanted British officers of the Indian Civil Service governed 300 million people through Indian clerks, police, revenue collectors and soldiers.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Calcutta to 1911, then New Delhi, under the India Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Elected Indian representation came late and narrow: separate electorates from 1909, roughly 3% of adults enfranchised after 1919, about 14% under the Act of 1935. Universal suffrage came only with independence.
statusPeriods.note: The 565 princely states were never British territory. They kept their rulers under 'paramountcy', and are modelled here as separate territories nested inside British India.

departures.how: Britain, bankrupt after the war and unable to govern without Indian cooperation it no longer had, brought its own deadline forward by ten months and left in seventy-three days, splitting the country along a line nobody had seen.

led.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
led.role: Congress leader; first Prime Minister of India

led.name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
led.role: Muslim League leader who demanded and won Pakistan and became its first Governor-General

led.name: Mohandas Gandhi
led.role: led three decades of mass non-violent resistance, opposed partition, and spent 15 August 1947 fasting in Calcutta rather than at the ceremony

led.name: B. R. Ambedkar
led.role: Dalit leader and law minister who chaired the drafting committee of India's constitution

led.name: Vallabhbhai Patel
led.role: Congress leader who assembled 500-odd princely states into India in eighteen months

led.name: Louis Mountbatten
led.role: last Viceroy, who moved the date from June 1948 to August 1947

led.name: Cyril Radcliffe
led.role: London barrister who drew the border in about five weeks, having never been east of Suez

led.name: Clement Attlee
led.role: Prime Minister who set the deadline and chose to go rather than pay to stay

departures.movement: Indian National Congress and the All-India Muslim League

cost.note: Nobody counted. The low figure is the contemporary official estimate, the high one the outer edge of scholarly estimates; most historians now work with several hundred thousand to about a million. The displacement was the largest forced migration in recorded history. Tens of thousands of women were abducted, and both new states later organised their forcible 'recovery'.

warrant.author: Yasmin Khan
warrant.work: The Great Partition: The Making of India and Pakistan
warrant.supports: The speed of the transfer, the violence, and the displacement figures.
warrant.check: Yale University Press

departures.borders: Radcliffe cut Punjab and Bengal in two on maps in Delhi, using out-of-date census returns; his award was finished on 12 August and published on 17 August, so for two days after independence millions did not know which country they were in.

instrument.name: Indian Independence Act 1947
instrument.note: Royal assent on 18 July 1947; the transfer took effect at midnight between 14 and 15 August. Pakistan dates its independence from 14 August, India from 15 August, for the same moment.

contested.note: Responsibility is genuinely disputed. Ayesha Jalal argues Jinnah used the demand for Pakistan as a bargaining counter he never expected to be granted; others hold Congress refusal of a loose federation decisive; others again blame a British exit so rushed that no orderly transfer was possible. The death toll is disputed for the simplest reason: no authority was counting.

statusPeriods.franchise: A legislature came only in 1932; the tribal agencies never had one. Congress, through the Khudai Khidmatgar, won the provincial elections of 1937 and 1946.
statusPeriods.note: Between 1849 and 1947 British and Indian troops mounted well over fifty punitive expeditions into the hills. The 1936-39 Waziristan campaign tied down some 40,000 troops.

departures.how: A referendum offering only India or Pakistan, with no option for an independent Pashtunistan, was boycotted by the governing Congress ministry; 289,244 votes were cast for Pakistan out of an electorate of about 573,000.

territories.name: Balochistan and Kalat

modernSuccessors.name: Pakistan
modernSuccessors.note: Pakistan's largest province by area and smallest by population; Kalat acceded only in March 1948.

geoCoverage.label: A garrison, a railway and four princely states
geoCoverage.change: Britain held Quetta, the Bolan pass and the railway to the Afghan border directly from the Treaty of Jacobabad in December 1876, and left the rest to the Khan of Kalat and the sardars under a Political Agent. It is hatched because most of it was never administered.

acquisitions.how: Robert Sandeman settled the quarrel between the Khan of Kalat and his sardars by paying both, and took a British garrison into Quetta as the price of the arbitration.

counterparties.name: Khanate of Kalat
counterparties.lost: Its foreign relations, and Quetta, leased to Britain and never given back. The Khan gained a subsidy and British backing against his own nobles.

counterparties.name: The Baloch and Brahui sardars
counterparties.lost: Independent action, in exchange for allowances and British recognition of their power over their own tribesmen.

people.name: Robert Sandeman
people.role: Political Agent whose system of paying Baloch sardars became the model for the whole frontier

people.name: Khudadad Khan
people.role: Khan of Kalat, who signed and was later deposed by the British in 1893

acquisitions.how: The Treaty of Gandamak, imposed on Afghanistan in the middle of a war, transferred Pishin, Sibi and the Khyber and Michni passes to British administration.

counterparties.name: The Emirate of Afghanistan
counterparties.lost: The districts commanding the passes into India, and control of its own foreign policy, which Britain took over entirely.

statusPeriods.label: Agency rule: subsidies, jirgas and a railway
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: An Agent to the Governor-General at Quetta ran the leased and ceded districts directly and dealt with Kalat, Las Bela, Kharan and Makran through their rulers, paying sardars to keep the passes and the railway open.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Quetta, under the Government of India directly
statusPeriods.franchise: No legislature and no vote of any kind until 1947; decisions were taken by a Shahi Jirga of nominated sardars.

departures.how: The Shahi Jirga of nominated sardars and the Quetta municipality voted for Pakistan on 29 June 1947; the Khan of Kalat declared independence on 12 August 1947 and was made to accede on 27 March 1948 after Pakistani troops moved in.

led.name: Mir Ahmad Yar Khan
led.role: Khan of Kalat, who declared independence and signed accession seven months later

led.name: Prince Abdul Karim
led.role: the Khan's brother, who led the first Baloch insurgency against accession in 1948

led.role: had been Kalat's own legal adviser before becoming Pakistan's Governor-General

cost.note: The 1948 accession was enforced without a battle, but it began a cycle of Baloch insurgencies in 1948, 1958, 1962, 1973 and after 2004 whose casualties have never been reliably counted.

departures.borders: Britain's frontier engineering survived intact: the Goldsmid Line of 1871 to Persia and the Durand Line of 1893 to Afghanistan became Pakistan's western borders, and Kalat's leased districts were simply transferred.

contested.note: Whether Kalat was ever part of India, and so whether it had a right to independence in 1947, is genuinely disputed. Britain treated it as a state in treaty relations, but the lapse of paramountcy left its status unresolved, and Baloch nationalists still argue accession was coerced.

partition.note: Balochistan joined Pakistan through a jirga of nominated sardars, not a popular vote, and Kalat's accession followed a military move.
partition.lineDrawnBy: No new line was drawn; Britain's Goldsmid and Durand lines were inherited

violence.note: Insurgency in Balochistan began in 1948 within months of accession and has recurred five times since.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Sind-Pishin railway and the Quetta cantonment were built to move troops to Kandahar, not to develop the province, and Balochistan remains the poorest part of Pakistan.

misconception.belief: British India was a single administered territory with one system of law.

territories.name: Assam
territories.formalName: The Province of Assam and its hill districts

namesOverTime.name: The Ahom kingdom
namesOverTime.note: Ruled the Brahmaputra valley for nearly 600 years and turned back seventeen Mughal invasions before Burma broke it.

namesOverTime.name: Assam and the states of the Indian north-east, and the Sylhet division of Bangladesh
namesOverTime.note: Colonial Assam has since been divided into Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh, with Sylhet in Bangladesh.

modernSuccessors.name: India
modernSuccessors.note: Divided since into Assam, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh.

modernSuccessors.name: Bangladesh
modernSuccessors.note: Sylhet voted in July 1947 to leave Assam for East Bengal.

geoCoverage.label: The Brahmaputra valley and the hills around it
geoCoverage.change: Burma gave up Assam at Yandabo. The valley was administered from Bengal; the Naga, Lushai, Garo and Abor hills were claimed on paper and entered only by punitive column.

geoCoverage.label: A province, with Sylhet attached
geoCoverage.change: Assam was made a separate Chief Commissioner's province and Bengali-speaking Sylhet was attached to it to make it financially viable, a decision Assamese and Sylhetis both resented for seventy-three years.

acquisitions.how: Company columns drove the Burmese army out of Assam in 1825; Burma, which had overrun the province in 1817-21 and killed or driven out a large part of its population, signed it away at Yandabo the following February. The Ahom dynasty, which had not been at the table, was pensioned off within twelve years.

counterparties.name: Konbaung kingdom of Burma
counterparties.lost: Assam, Manipur, Cachar and Jaintia, conquests it had held for less than a decade.

counterparties.name: The Ahom kingdom
counterparties.lost: Six hundred years of independence. Purandar Singha was restored as a client king in 1833 and deposed in 1838 for failing to pay tribute.

counterparties.name: The Naga, Lushai, Garo, Khasi and Abor peoples
counterparties.lost: Their hills were declared British by a treaty signed 1,500 km away, and then invaded repeatedly for the next seventy years.

acquisitions.resistance: The Khasi under U Tirot Sing fought a four-year war from 1829; the Angami Naga held out at Khonoma until 1879-80; the Lushai hills were not annexed until 1895.

acquisitions.how: Assam was cut out of Bengal as a separate province, and Bengali-speaking Sylhet was transferred into it against local petitions, purely to give the new province enough revenue to pay for itself.

counterparties.name: The people of Sylhet
counterparties.lost: Their place in Bengal. Sylhetis petitioned against the transfer in 1874, again in 1905 and again in 1912, and finally voted their way out in 1947.

statusPeriods.label: A Bengal frontier district turned tea garden
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Company officers governed the valley from Gauhati under Bengal; from 1838 the tea industry was opened to private planters who were granted waste land on terms designed to attract British capital.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Gauhati, under Fort William in Calcutta

statusPeriods.label: Tea, labour and excluded hills
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Chief Commissioner, from 1921 a Governor, ruled the valley; the hill districts were 'excluded areas' where the provincial legislature had no power and missionaries and political officers did.
statusPeriods.franchise: Property-qualified with separate electorates; the province had Congress and Muslim League ministries alternating from 1937. Tea-garden labourers, about a sixth of the population, were effectively unenfranchised.

statusPeriods.label: The front line against Japan
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Assam became the base for the Burma campaign and the airlift over the Hump to China; the Japanese and the Indian National Army reached Kohima and Imphal in 1944 and were stopped there.
statusPeriods.note: Congress ministers had resigned in 1939 and the Quit India arrests of 1942 removed most of the province's elected politicians.

statusPeriods.label: The last two years
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Gopinath Bordoloi's Congress ministry governed and fought off a Cabinet Mission plan that would have grouped Assam with Bengal in a Muslim-majority bloc.

departures.how: Assam went to India, but Sylhet was taken out of it by referendum on 6 and 7 July 1947 and given to East Bengal, taking about a sixth of the province's population with it.

led.name: Gopinath Bordoloi
led.role: Congress premier who kept Assam out of the Muslim-majority grouping proposed by the Cabinet Mission

led.name: A. K. Fazlul Huq
led.role: Bengali leader whose party had earlier governed with Assamese Muslim support

led.role: Naga leader who declared Naga independence on 14 August 1947, a day before India's

cost.note: The referendum passed off peacefully. The unresolved question was the hills: the Naga National Council declared independence on 14 August 1947 and the insurgency that followed has run, with ceasefires, ever since.

departures.borders: The Sylhet referendum moved a boundary by vote rather than by commission, one of only two places in India where that happened; the McMahon Line of 1914, which Britain drew with Tibet, became India's disputed border with China.

consequences.borderLegacy: The McMahon Line and the 'excluded areas' policy left independent India with contested frontiers with China and with a north-east administered under special constitutional provisions.

pedagogy.hook: Britain took Assam in 1826, found tea growing wild there in 1823, and within thirty years had built an industry worked by a million indentured labourers shipped in from a thousand kilometres away.

misconception.belief: Tea is originally Chinese and the British simply brought the plant to India.
misconception.correction: Camellia sinensis var. assamica grows wild in Assam and was drunk by the Singpho people there long before any planter arrived. Robert Bruce recorded it in 1823. What Britain brought was not the plant but the plantation: land grants, a criminal labour law, and a recruiting network that carried labourers from Chota Nagpur to gardens they could be jailed for leaving.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Assam packs the whole imperial pattern into one province: conquest by treaty, a cash crop, imported bonded labour, hill peoples excluded from the state, and a border question left unsolved in 1947 that is still being fought over.

modernSuccessors.name: India

acquisitions.how: The Nizam of Hyderabad could not pay the arrears on the troops Britain stationed in his state, so Berar, his richest cotton district, was assigned to Britain to cover the bill.

counterparties.lost: Berar's cotton revenue. Hyderabad went on claiming it back for eighty years and never got it; in 1902 the assignment was converted into a perpetual lease.

instrument.name: Treaty of 1853 assigning Berar
instrument.note: Converted to a perpetual lease at 25 lakh rupees a year by agreement with Curzon in 1902; Berar was then administered with the Central Provinces.

counterparties.lost: Its existence. Hindu law permitted adoption to continue a line; Dalhousie ruled that a dependent state needed British consent, which he withheld.

counterparties.name: Baka Bai, the dowager rani

people.name: James Broun-Ramsay, Lord Dalhousie

statusPeriods.label: Cotton, forest and famine
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Chief Commissioner, later Governor, ruled from Nagpur; the Forest Acts of 1865 and 1878 turned Gond and Baiga woodland into state reserve and made customary use of it a crime.
statusPeriods.franchise: Property-qualified from 1919; a Congress ministry under N. B. Khare took office in 1937.

acquisitions.how: Two hundred prisoners from the 1857 rebellion were landed at Port Blair under guard to clear jungle for a penal colony, on islands whose people had driven off every previous attempt.

people.role: Indian revolutionary held in the Cellular Jail from 1911 to 1921, who petitioned repeatedly for release

counterparties.lost: Sovereignty over islands they had held through three failed European colonisation attempts; a penal station was placed on Great Nicobar.

statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Blair, under the Government of India
statusPeriods.franchise: None. The population consisted of convicts, their guards, their descendants, and the islanders, none of whom voted.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan took the islands in March 1942 and ran them by military administration; hundreds of islanders were executed or tortured as suspected spies and many more died in a forced settlement on Havelock Island.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: British authority was zero for three and a half years: the islands were held by Japan, and formally handed by Japan to Subhas Chandra Bose's Provisional Government of Azad Hind in December 1943, though real power stayed with the Japanese navy.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Blair, under Japanese military administration
statusPeriods.note: Bose raised the Indian tricolour at Port Blair on 30 December 1943 and renamed the islands Shaheed and Swaraj. He was not shown the prison camps.

departures.how: Britain considered keeping the islands as a defence base and dropped the idea; they passed to India with the rest of the Indian Empire and became a Union Territory.

counterparties.lost: Half its territory, its dynasty and its independence. Tipu's family were deported and the state's French-trained army disbanded.

counterparties.name: The restored Wodeyar dynasty
counterparties.lost: Real sovereignty. They were given a throne on condition of paying a subsidy that consumed much of the revenue.

acquisitions.how: After a peasant revolt in Nagar against the state's tax demands, the Company removed Krishnaraja Wodeyar III from all power and administered Mysore directly for fifty years without deposing him.

statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bangalore, under the Commissioner for Mysore

Britain and China declare a protectorate over Sikkim

The monarchy abolished; Sikkim joins India

territories.name: Manipur
territories.formalName: The princely state of Manipur

modernSuccessors.name: India
modernSuccessors.note: A Union Territory from 1949 and a full state in 1972. The merger agreement of September 1949 is still disputed by Manipuri nationalists.

geoCoverage.label: A valley kingdom and the hills around it
geoCoverage.change: Restored to its raja at Yandabo as a British-protected state; the Meitei valley was administered through the palace, and the surrounding Naga and Kuki hills through a British Political Agent.

acquisitions.how: Burma renounced Manipur at Yandabo and the Company restored Gambhir Singh to the throne he had helped it win, on terms that gave Britain control of the kingdom's external relations.

counterparties.name: Konbaung kingdom of Burma
counterparties.lost: Manipur, which it had devastated in the Seven Years Devastation of 1819-26 when much of the population fled or was carried off.

counterparties.name: The kingdom of Manipur
counterparties.lost: Its foreign policy, and eventually its independence. It had been a sovereign kingdom with its own script, calendar and chronicle, the Cheitharol Kumbaba, kept since the twelfth century.

acquisitions.how: After a palace coup, a British attempt to arrest the commander-in-chief failed and five British officers were executed at Imphal; three columns invaded, took the capital, and hanged the prince Tikendrajit and General Thangal in public in August.

counterparties.name: The kingdom of Manipur
counterparties.lost: Its sovereignty. Britain declared the state forfeited by conquest, then installed a five-year-old boy as raja and ran the kingdom through a Political Agent.

counterparties.name: Prince Tikendrajit and General Thangal
counterparties.lost: Their lives. They were tried by a British court for waging war against the Queen and hanged at Imphal on 13 August 1891 in front of a crowd.

people.name: Bir Tikendrajit Singh
people.role: Senapati of Manipur; led the resistance and was hanged on 13 August 1891

people.name: Thangal General
people.role: Manipuri commander, hanged with Tikendrajit at the age of about 75

people.name: James Quinton
people.role: Chief Commissioner of Assam, executed by the Manipuris after the failed arrest

cost.note: The Anglo-Manipur War lasted about a month. British casualties were counted precisely and Manipuri ones were not; the figure is an estimate.

acquisitions.resistance: Manipuri troops beat off the first British attack at Imphal; the campaign that followed needed three converging columns from Assam, Cachar and Burma.

statusPeriods.label: An allied kingdom on the Burma road
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The raja governed and supplied troops for British campaigns in the hills; a Political Agent sat at Imphal from 1835 and intervened in successions.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Imphal, with a British Political Agent

statusPeriods.label: Conquered, then handed back to a child
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain declared the state forfeit, installed a five-year-old raja and governed through the Political Agent; the hill areas were administered separately from the valley, a division Manipur still lives with.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Imphal, under the Political Agent and the Government of Assam
statusPeriods.franchise: None until 1948. The Nupi Lan, or women's wars, of 1904 and 1939 were mass protests by Manipuri women against forced labour and rice exports, and the second forced the state to stop rice exports.

departures.how: Manipur resumed independence when paramountcy lapsed, adopted a constitution and elected an assembly by universal adult suffrage in 1948, and was merged into India in October 1949 after its maharaja signed under confinement at Shillong.

led.name: Bodhchandra Singh
led.role: last maharaja; signed the merger agreement at Shillong on 21 September 1949 while under Indian guard

led.name: Hijam Irabot
led.role: led the Nikhil Manipuri Mahasabha and the peasant movement, and went underground against the merger

led.name: Rani Gaidinliu
led.role: Naga spiritual and political leader of the Heraka movement, jailed by the British from 1932 to 1947

departures.movement: Nikhil Manipuri Mahasabha and the Manipur State Congress

cost.note: Nobody was killed in the 1949 merger. The insurgencies that followed from the 1960s, and the Armed Forces Special Powers Act imposed in 1958, have cost thousands of lives since, and remain contested ground.

departures.borders: The line Britain drew between Manipur and Burma cut Naga and Kuki communities in two, and the separate administration of hills and valley left a political division that has produced repeated conflict.

contested.note: Manipuri nationalists hold that the 1949 merger agreement is void because the maharaja signed it under confinement and without the consent of the elected assembly, which was dissolved. India treats it as a valid accession.

violence.note: The 1891 war ended with the public hanging of Tikendrajit and Thangal; in 1944 the Japanese and the Indian National Army besieged Imphal and roughly 12,000 Japanese and 12,500 Allied soldiers were killed or wounded in the battle.

populationTransfer.note: The Seven Years Devastation of 1819-26, before British protection, emptied much of the valley; refugees returned from Cachar and Sylhet in the following decades.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Manipur-Burma boundary and the hill and valley administrative split are the roots of the Naga, Kuki and Meitei conflicts that continue today.

peak.populationNote: 1941 census of Manipur State.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Manipur’s largest recorded population: 512,069 people, counted in 1941.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.

evidence.author: Gangmumei Kamei
evidence.work: A History of Modern Manipur
evidence.supports: The Anglo-Manipur War, the protectorate and the 1949 merger.

evidence.author: Sanjib Baruah
evidence.work: Durable Disorder: Understanding the Politics of Northeast India
evidence.supports: The consequences of the hill and valley administrative divide.

pedagogy.hook: In 1948 Manipur elected an assembly by universal adult suffrage, before India itself did; eighteen months later the kingdom was merged into India and the assembly dissolved.

misconception.belief: All of British India was ready for democracy only when Britain granted it.
misconception.correction: Manipur, a small Himalayan-foothill kingdom, wrote its own constitution in 1947 and held the first election in the region under universal adult franchise in June and July 1948, before India's own first general election in 1951-52. Its assembly was dissolved when the state merged into India in October 1949.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Manipur shows what happened at the edges of the empire: a sovereign kingdom conquered in a month in 1891, a public hanging that is still a day of mourning, and a merger in 1949 whose legality is still argued about.

keyDates.what: Yandabo restores Manipur under British protection
Tikendrajit and Thangal hanged in public at Imphal
Nupi Lan: Manipuri women stop the rice export trade
The battle of Imphal halts the Japanese and INA advance
Manipur merged into India

territories.name: Tripura
territories.formalName: Hill Tipperah: the princely state of Tripura

modernSuccessors.name: India
modernSuccessors.note: A Union Territory from 1949 and a full state in 1972.

geoCoverage.label: Hill Tipperah, a protected kingdom
geoCoverage.change: The Manikya dynasty kept its hill kingdom as a British-protected state, while its lowland estate of Chakla Roshnabad in Bengal was British territory it held as a private landlord.

acquisitions.how: With Burma's claims on the north-east extinguished at Yandabo, the Company confirmed the Manikya raja in his hill kingdom as a protected ruler, while taxing him as a Bengal landlord for his plains estate.

counterparties.name: The Manikya kingdom of Tripura
counterparties.lost: Its independence in external affairs, and the ambiguity that let it be simultaneously a sovereign in the hills and a subject landholder in the plains.

counterparties.name: Konbaung kingdom of Burma
counterparties.lost: Its claims over Cachar, Jaintia and the country west of Manipur.

contested.note: There is no single instrument making Tripura a protected state; its status grew out of Company practice from the 1760s onwards and was settled by usage rather than by treaty. 1826 is used here as the date its neighbourhood was fixed.

statusPeriods.label: A raja in the hills, a zamindar in the plains
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Manikya ruler governed his hill kingdom and simultaneously paid land revenue to the Company for his Bengal estate, so the same man was a sovereign on one side of a line and a taxpayer on the other.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Agartala, under the Government of Bengal

statusPeriods.label: Hill Tipperah under paramountcy
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The maharaja ruled through his own officials under a Political Agent at Agartala; Bengali cultivators were encouraged into the state's lowlands, and the indigenous Tripuri population became a shrinking share of it.
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Maharaja Bir Bikram set up a limited advisory council in the 1940s and reserved land for the indigenous Tripuris in 1943, a reservation later swamped by refugee settlement.

departures.how: Paramountcy lapsed while the maharaja was dying; his widow Kanchan Prava Devi governed as regent and signed the merger with India in September 1949, with East Bengal now surrounding the state on three sides.

led.name: Kanchan Prava Devi
led.role: Regent Maharani who governed after her husband's death and signed the merger agreement with India

led.name: Bir Bikram Kishore Manikya
led.role: maharaja who died on 17 May 1947, three months before paramountcy lapsed

led.name: Dasarath Deb
led.role: led the Jana Shiksha Samiti, a Tripuri education and rights movement and later became chief minister of Tripura

departures.movement: Tripura Rajya Praja Mandal and the Jana Shiksha Samiti

cost.note: Partition made Tripura a pocket almost surrounded by East Pakistan; refugee arrivals between 1947 and 1971 turned the indigenous Tripuri population into a minority in their own state. Figures come from Indian census comparisons.

warrant.author: The Census of India
warrant.work: Census of India: the 1951, 1961 and 1971 counts for Tripura compared
warrant.supports: Partition made Tripura a pocket almost surrounded by East Pakistan; refugee arrivals between 1947 and 1971 turned the indigenous Tripuri population into a minority in their own state. Figures come from Indian census comparisons.
warrant.check: Census of India, Office of the Registrar General, New Delhi.
warrant.note: The refugee arrivals are read off the difference between three censuses, not counted at the border.

departures.borders: Radcliffe's line left Tripura connected to India by a single narrow corridor through Assam, and the state's road distance to Calcutta went from about 350 km to over 1,700 km overnight.

populationTransfer.note: Bengali settlement encouraged by the state before 1947, and refugee arrivals from East Bengal after it, reduced the indigenous Tripuri share of the population from a majority to under a third by 1971.

consequences.borderLegacy: The partition line boxed Tripura in on three sides and made it dependent on a corridor through Assam, which is why the north-east's connectivity is still a live political question.

violence.note: The demographic change produced an insurgency from the 1970s in which the Tripuri National Volunteers and later the National Liberation Front of Tripura fought the Indian state.

peak.populationNote: 1941 census of Tripura State (Hill Tipperah).

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Tripura’s largest recorded population: 513,010 people, counted in 1941.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Sanjib Baruah
evidence.work: Durable Disorder: Understanding the Politics of Northeast India
evidence.supports: Partition's effect on the north-east and the demographic transformation of Tripura.

pedagogy.hook: Partition turned Tripura from a state 350 km from Calcutta into one over 1,700 km away by road, without moving it an inch.

misconception.belief: Partition only affected Punjab and Bengal.
misconception.correction: It reshaped the whole north-east. Tripura was left almost surrounded by East Pakistan; Assam lost Sylhet by referendum; the road and rail links from the region to the rest of India were cut and replaced by a corridor twenty kilometres wide. The refugee flow into Tripura made its indigenous people a minority within a generation.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows partition as a geography problem as well as a human one: lines drawn on a map in Delhi cut roads, rivers and railways that whole regions depended on.

Land reserved for indigenous Tripuris by royal order
Paramountcy lapses; East Bengal surrounds the state
Tripura merged into India

territories.name: Ceylon
territories.formalName: The Crown Colony of Ceylon

from.note: A rough marker: the island's own name in Sinhala and Sanskrit sources long predates any European contact and has no single starting date.

namesOverTime.name: Sri Lanka
namesOverTime.note: Adopted with the republican constitution of 1972.

modernSuccessors.name: Sri Lanka
modernSuccessors.note: A dominion from 1948 and a republic under the name Sri Lanka from 22 May 1972.

geoCoverage.label: The Dutch coastal provinces
geoCoverage.change: Britain took the Dutch company's forts and cinnamon lands while the Netherlands was under French control, and administered them at first from Madras.

geoCoverage.label: The whole island
geoCoverage.change: The Kandyan Convention deposed the king of Kandy and gave Britain the interior, which no European power had held in 300 years of trying.

acquisitions.how: With the Netherlands occupied by France, a Madras expedition took Trincomalee and then Colombo from the Dutch East India Company, whose garrisons mostly surrendered without a fight.

counterparties.name: The Dutch East India Company
counterparties.lost: Its cinnamon monopoly and its forts, taken while its home country was a French client republic.

counterparties.name: The coastal Sinhalese, Tamil and Moor communities
counterparties.lost: One European ruler for another. The Madras administration's first act was to raise the taxes, which set off a rebellion in 1797.

acquisitions.how: The Treaty of Amiens made the Dutch cession permanent, and Ceylon became the first Crown colony in Asia, run from London rather than by the East India Company.

counterparties.name: The Batavian Republic
counterparties.lost: Ceylon permanently, in a peace treaty that returned most other Dutch colonies but not this one.

acquisitions.how: Kandyan chiefs, in revolt against their own king's cruelty, signed a convention with the British that deposed Sri Vikrama Rajasinha, handed sovereignty to the Crown and promised to protect Buddhism.

counterparties.name: The Kandyan kingdom
counterparties.lost: Its independence, after resisting the Portuguese, the Dutch and one British invasion in 1803. Its last king, of the Tamil Nayak line, was exiled to Vellore in India.

counterparties.name: The Kandyan aristocracy
counterparties.lost: The convention promised them their offices and privileges; within two years Britain was ignoring the promise, which is why they rose in 1817.

instrument.name: The Kandyan Convention
instrument.note: Clause 5 pledged that the religion of the Buddha would be maintained and protected, a promise British missionary policy later broke and that Sinhala politics has cited ever since.

people.name: Sri Vikrama Rajasinha
people.role: last king of Kandy, deposed and exiled to Vellore, where he died in 1832

people.name: Ehelepola Nilame
people.role: Kandyan first minister who allied with the British after the king had his wife and children executed

people.name: Robert Brownrigg
people.role: Governor who negotiated the convention and then crushed the rebellion of 1817-18

acquisitions.resistance: The Uva-Wellassa rebellion of 1817-18 was put down by burning villages, killing cattle and destroying irrigation tanks and paddy across the province; Keppetipola Disawe was beheaded in November 1818.

statusPeriods.label: Military occupation, administered from Madras
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The East India Company ran the coast from Madras and applied its revenue methods, which provoked a rebellion in 1797 and got the island transferred to the Crown instead.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Colombo, under the Government of Madras

statusPeriods.label: The first British Crown colony in Asia
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Governor appointed in London ruled with a nominated council; the Colebrooke-Cameron reforms of 1833 unified the island's administration, opened land to plantations and made English the language of government.
statusPeriods.franchise: A tiny elected element from 1912 on a literacy and property test; fewer than 4% of adults could vote before 1931.

statusPeriods.label: Universal suffrage under a British Governor
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Donoughmore constitution gave every adult a vote and put elected members in charge of departments through executive committees, while the Governor kept defence, foreign affairs and a veto.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage for men and women over 21 from 1931, the first grant of its kind anywhere in Asia and only three years after women in Britain got the vote on equal terms.

statusPeriods.label: Soulbury constitution: internal self-government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: D. S. Senanayake formed a government under the Soulbury constitution with a cabinet responsible to an elected parliament, four months before formal independence.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage.

departures.how: Ceylon became a dominion by agreement, without a mass campaign, a boycott or a shot fired, six months after India and Pakistan and on terms that kept British naval and air bases at Trincomalee and Katunayake.

led.name: D. S. Senanayake
led.role: negotiated independence and became the first Prime Minister; his government then disenfranchised the Indian Tamil plantation population

led.name: Ponnambalam Arunachalam
led.role: founded the Ceylon National Congress in 1919 and resigned from it over Tamil representation

led.name: A. E. Goonesinha
led.role: trade union leader whose strikes in the 1920s and 1930s forced political concessions

led.name: Sir Henry Monck-Mason Moore
led.role: last British Governor, who handed over to a Governor-General on 4 February 1948

departures.movement: Ceylon National Congress and the United National Party

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. The cost fell afterwards on the Indian Tamil plantation workers: the Citizenship Act of 1948 and the Franchise Act of 1949 stripped citizenship and the vote from around 700,000 people whose families had worked the tea estates for generations.

departures.borders: No borders changed. The lines that mattered were legal ones: who counted as a citizen, and whose language the state would use, questions that led to the Sinhala Only Act of 1956 and eventually to civil war.

evidence.author: K. M. de Silva
evidence.work: A History of Sri Lanka
evidence.supports: The constitutional route to independence and the citizenship legislation that followed.

populationTransfer.note: Around a million Tamil labourers were recruited from southern India for the coffee and then tea estates between the 1830s and 1930s, and their descendants were left stateless by the laws of 1948 and 1949.

violence.note: The Uva-Wellassa rebellion of 1817-18 was suppressed by destroying the food supply of a whole province; the Matale rebellion of 1848 was put down with martial law and summary executions.

toll.note: Estimates for deaths in and after the 1817-18 rebellion, mostly from the destruction of paddy fields, tanks and cattle rather than from fighting. No count was made and the figures are reconstructions.

commonwealth.note: A realm until it became the republic of Sri Lanka on 22 May 1972; still a Commonwealth member.

consequences.economicLegacy: Coffee, then tea after the leaf blight of the 1870s, made Ceylon a plantation economy owned largely from London and worked by imported labour; tea is still the country's signature export.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English replaced Sinhala and Tamil in government in 1833 and the reaction against it produced the Sinhala Only Act of 1956, the grievance at the root of the civil war of 1983-2009.

peak.populationNote: 1946 census, the last under British rule.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Ceylon’s largest recorded population: 6,657,339 people, counted in 1946.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: K. M. de Silva
evidence.work: A History of Sri Lanka
evidence.supports: The whole span from the Dutch cession to independence.

evidence.author: Nira Wickramasinghe
evidence.work: Sri Lanka in the Modern Age: A History
evidence.supports: Colonial society, the plantation economy and the politics of citizenship after 1948.

pedagogy.hook: Ceylon gave every adult the vote in 1931, seventeen years before independence and before any other country in Asia.

misconception.belief: Independence meant everyone in the colony became a citizen of the new country.
misconception.correction: Within months of independence Ceylon's parliament passed a Citizenship Act and a Franchise Act that left around 700,000 Indian Tamil plantation workers stateless and voteless, though many families had been on the island for a century. Deciding who belongs is a decision the new state makes, and it does not always include everyone the empire brought.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Ceylon is the counter-example to India: the same empire, next door, leaving six months later, with no partition, no massacre and a negotiated handover, and with damage that showed up in the citizenship law instead.

keyDates.what: Britain takes the Dutch coastal provinces
Kandyan Convention: the interior falls at last
Uva-Wellassa rebellion crushed by destroying the harvest
Universal adult suffrage, the first in Asia
Independence as a dominion

territories.name: British Burma
territories.formalName: Burma: a province of British India, then a separate colony

modernSuccessors.name: Myanmar
modernSuccessors.note: Independent as the Union of Burma; renamed Myanmar by the military government in 1989, a change many governments and Burmese opposition groups did not accept.

geoCoverage.label: The two coasts
geoCoverage.change: Yandabo gave Britain Arakan and Tenasserim, the coasts on either side of the Burmese heartland, and left the kingdom its river and its capital.

geoCoverage.label: Lower Burma: the delta and the ports
geoCoverage.change: Dalhousie annexed Pegu by proclamation after a dispute over harbour dues, without a treaty. Burma was now landlocked and the rice delta was British.

geoCoverage.label: The whole country
geoCoverage.change: Upper Burma annexed and the monarchy abolished. The Shan, Kachin, Chin and Karenni areas are hatched: they were administered separately as Frontier Areas, never under the Burmese ministry, which is why 1947 needed the Panglong Agreement.

acquisitions.how: Company forces took Arakan and Tenasserim in the field in 1824-25 and sat in Rangoon until the Konbaung court signed at Yandabo, giving up both provinces plus Assam and Manipur and a million pounds it raised by taxing its own people twice.

counterparties.name: The Konbaung kingdom
counterparties.lost: Its western conquests, its western coast and its solvency. The indemnity was worth several years of royal revenue.

counterparties.name: The Rakhine (Arakanese) people
counterparties.lost: They had already lost their kingdom to Burma in 1785; in 1826 they exchanged a Burmese ruler for a British one and became a frontier district of Bengal.

cost.money: About 13 million pounds to Britain, the most expensive war the East India Company had yet fought.
cost.note: Most British and Indian deaths were from disease. Burmese losses were never counted, and the range covers all sides.

acquisitions.how: Two British sea captains complained about harbour dues at Rangoon; a squadron was sent to demand compensation, the demands escalated, and Dalhousie annexed the province of Pegu by proclamation without offering a treaty.

counterparties.name: The Konbaung kingdom
counterparties.lost: The Irrawaddy delta, Rangoon and its access to the sea. King Pagan Min was overthrown by his own brother for losing them.

counterparties.name: The Mon and Karen people of the delta
counterparties.lost: The war and the annexation redrew their world; Karen communities allied with the British and with missionaries, a choice that shaped the country's politics for the next century.

acquisitions.how: A fine imposed on a British timber company became the pretext for an eleven-day war; King Thibaw surrendered Mandalay, was put on a steamer to India, and on New Year's Day 1886 his kingdom was declared part of British India.

counterparties.name: The Konbaung kingdom
counterparties.lost: Its monarchy, abolished by proclamation. Thibaw and Supayalat died in exile at Ratnagiri; the throne room's contents were shipped to museums.

counterparties.name: The Shan, Kachin, Chin and Karenni polities
counterparties.lost: They had been tributaries, not subjects; Britain declared them British and then spent a decade subduing them one valley at a time.

people.name: Thibaw Min
people.role: last king of Burma, exiled to India in November 1885

people.name: Supayalat
people.role: his queen, who went into exile with him and returned to Burma only after his death

people.name: Randolph Churchill
people.role: Secretary of State for India who pushed the annexation and timed the proclamation for New Year's Day as a present for the Queen

cost.note: The war itself cost few lives; the campaign to break the resistance that followed took five years, 30,000 troops and an unknown number of Burmese lives. British reports classified the resistance as dacoity, so its dead were counted as criminals.

warrant.author: The British administration of Upper Burma, in its own reports
warrant.work: British reports on the pacification of Upper Burma, 1886–90
warrant.supports: The war itself cost few lives; the campaign to break the resistance that followed took five years, 30,000 troops and an unknown number of Burmese lives. British reports classified the resistance as dacoity, so its dead were counted as criminals.
warrant.check: East India Company and Government of India military returns are in the India Office Records at the British Library (IOR series) and in the WO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: British reports classified the resistance as dacoity, so its dead were counted as criminals where they were counted at all.

acquisitions.resistance: Guerrilla resistance under local leaders and former royal officials went on until about 1890, and the Saya San rebellion of 1930-32 showed it had not been forgotten.

statusPeriods.label: Coastal districts of British India
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Arakan and Tenasserim were run as frontier commissionerships under Bengal, and Pegu was added in 1852; the priority was teak, rice and the coast, not the people on it.

statusPeriods.label: A province of British India
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Burma was governed as an Indian province from Rangoon; Indian clerks, soldiers, moneylenders and labourers came with the administration, and by the 1930s Rangoon had an Indian-born majority.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Rangoon, under the Government of India
statusPeriods.franchise: A legislative council with elected members from 1923 under dyarchy; the Frontier Areas were excluded from it entirely.

statusPeriods.label: A separate colony at last
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Burma got its own Governor, cabinet and legislature under the Government of Burma Act 1935; Ba Maw and then U Saw headed ministries while the Governor kept defence, foreign affairs and the Frontier Areas.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Rangoon, under the Burma Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: About 13% of adults could vote for the House of Representatives; separate seats were reserved for Indians, Karens, Anglo-Burmans and the business chambers.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan drove the British out in four months, declared Burma independent under Ba Maw on 1 August 1943, and kept the real decisions with the Japanese army; Aung San's Burma Independence Army changed sides in March 1945.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: British authority was nil for three years: the government sat in exile at Simla while Japan and a nominally independent Burmese state held the country.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Rangoon, under Japanese military authority; the British government-in-exile at Simla
statusPeriods.note: Between 400,000 and 600,000 Indians fled overland to Assam in 1942; estimates of those who died on the roads range from 10,000 to 80,000.

statusPeriods.label: Reoccupied and negotiating out
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain returned to a country whose only functioning political force was the Anti-Fascist People's Freedom League, and after a general strike in 1946 negotiated a handover in London in January 1947.

departures.how: Attlee and Aung San agreed independence in London in January 1947; Aung San was assassinated six months later, and Burma left on 4 January 1948 at an hour chosen by astrologers, outside the Commonwealth.

led.name: Aung San
led.role: led the Burma Independence Army, changed sides in 1945, negotiated independence, and was assassinated with six colleagues on 19 July 1947

led.name: U Nu
led.role: took over after the assassination and became the first Prime Minister

led.name: Sao Shwe Thaik
led.role: Shan ruler of Yawnghwe who signed the Panglong Agreement and became Burma's first President

led.name: U Saw
led.role: former premier convicted of organising the assassination of Aung San and hanged in 1948

led.name: Clement Attlee
led.role: Prime Minister who agreed the timetable in January 1947

departures.movement: Anti-Fascist People's Freedom League

cost.note: Burma was the only part of the Indian Empire fought over from end to end. Estimates of Burmese civilian war deaths from 1942 to 1945 range widely; the ranges here follow standard reference works and are not precise.

departures.borders: The Panglong Agreement of 12 February 1947 brought the Shan, Kachin and Chin into the union with a promised right of secession after ten years; the Karen were not at Panglong, and the civil war that began in 1949 is the longest running in the world.

evidence.author: Michael W. Charney
evidence.work: A History of Modern Burma
evidence.supports: The separation of 1937, the occupation, Panglong and independence.

violence.note: Breaking the guerrilla resistance in Upper Burma after 1886 took five years and 30,000 troops; the Saya San rebellion of 1930-32 was suppressed with about 1,300 killed and 128 executed; the Second World War was fought across the whole country.
