populationTransfer.note: Indian migration under the open border with British India made Rangoon a majority-Indian city by 1931; the Japanese invasion sent 400,000 to 600,000 Indians fleeing overland to Assam in 1942, and tens of thousands died on the way.

commonwealth.note: Burma is the only major former British possession in Asia that refused to join the Commonwealth, on the grounds that a republic should not associate with a monarchy. India solved the same problem in 1949 by inventing the republican Commonwealth.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Irrawaddy delta was turned into the world's largest rice exporter after 1852 by Burmese cultivators borrowing from Indian Chettiar moneylenders; when prices collapsed in 1930 the lenders foreclosed and roughly half the delta's paddy land ended up in their hands.
consequences.borderLegacy: Administering the hills separately from the plains left a state that has never agreed on what it is, and the Frontier Areas question of 1947 is still being fought over.

peak.populationNote: 1941 census of Burma, taken four years after separation from India.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: British Burma’s largest recorded population: 16,823,798 people, counted in 1941.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Michael W. Charney
evidence.work: A History of Modern Burma
evidence.supports: The conquest, the colonial economy, the occupation and independence.

evidence.author: Thant Myint-U
evidence.work: The Making of Modern Burma
evidence.supports: The Konbaung state, the annexation of 1885-86 and the destruction of Burmese administration.

pedagogy.hook: Britain abolished the Burmese monarchy on New Year's Day 1886 and timed the proclamation as a present for Queen Victoria.

misconception.belief: Burma was a British colony like Kenya or Nigeria from the start.
misconception.correction: For 111 years Burma was governed as a province of British India, not as a colony of its own. Indian troops conquered it, Indian clerks administered it, Indian labourers built Rangoon and Indian moneylenders financed its rice. It was separated on 1 April 1937, and Burmese nationalists suspected a trick to keep it out of Indian independence.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Burma is the empire's clearest case of a state destroyed rather than governed: the monarchy abolished, the hills administered separately, and a country left in 1948 with a civil war that has never ended.

keyDates.what: Yandabo takes the two coasts
Pegu annexed; Burma loses the sea
The monarchy abolished; Burma joins British India
Burma separated from India as its own colony
Panglong Agreement brings the hill peoples into the union
Independence, outside the Commonwealth

territories.name: Nepal
territories.formalName: The Kingdom of Nepal under British treaty

modernSuccessors.name: Nepal
modernSuccessors.note: A monarchy until 2008, then a federal republic. Nepal was never colonised, which is a national fact as well as a historical one.

geoCoverage.label: Independent, but not free to act
geoCoverage.change: After the Anglo-Nepalese War, Nepal kept its independence, lost a third of its territory and accepted a British Resident in Kathmandu with control over its foreign dealings.

acquisitions.how: Two years of hard mountain fighting ended with Nepal ceding Kumaon, Garhwal, Sikkim's Terai and much of the western hills, accepting a British Resident, and agreeing to take no European into its service.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Nepal
counterparties.lost: About a third of its territory and the right to conduct its own foreign relations, though never its internal sovereignty or its independence in law.

counterparties.name: The people of Kumaon, Garhwal and the Terai
counterparties.lost: They changed rulers, from a Gorkha conquest state that had taken them thirty years earlier to the East India Company.

instrument.name: Treaty of Sugauli
instrument.note: Signed 2 December 1815 and ratified 4 March 1816. The atlas dates the change from ratification.

people.name: Bhimsen Thapa
people.role: Nepal's prime minister who fought the war and survived it in office for another twenty years

people.name: Amar Singh Thapa
people.role: commander whose defence of the western hills impressed the British enough to start recruiting Gurkhas

people.name: David Ochterlony
people.role: British commander in the war and the first Resident at Kathmandu

cost.note: Combined losses in the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814-16, mostly from disease and mountain fighting. Neither side counted the other's dead.

acquisitions.resistance: Nepali forces beat British columns repeatedly in 1814-15 at Nalapani and Jaithak; the Company won the war by weight of numbers and by taking the Terai supply base, not by any battlefield superiority.

statusPeriods.label: Independent, watched, and recruited from
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British Resident sat in Kathmandu and Nepal dealt with no other power; the Rana prime ministers who ruled from 1846 kept British goodwill by supplying soldiers, and Britain left the internal government alone.
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Nepal was ruled by hereditary Rana prime ministers from 1846 to 1951, with the Shah kings kept as figureheads.
statusPeriods.note: Nepal sent troops to help Britain in 1857, in both world wars and in Burma. Around 200,000 Nepalis served in the First World War and roughly 250,000 in the Second.

departures.how: Britain signed a treaty of friendship formally recognising Nepal's independence, a reward for the Gurkha divisions that had fought in France, Mesopotamia and Gallipoli.

led.name: Chandra Shumsher Jang Bahadur Rana
led.role: Rana prime minister who negotiated the 1923 treaty and traded soldiers for recognition

led.name: William Frederick O'Connor
led.role: British envoy who signed the treaty at Kathmandu

departures.movement: The Rana government of Nepal

cost.note: Nobody died in 1923. Nepal's price had been paid earlier: about 20,000 Nepali soldiers were killed serving in the British Indian Army in the First World War.

departures.borders: The Sugauli line of 1816 is still Nepal's border with India, and the Kalapani sector at its western end is disputed between the two countries today.

instrument.name: Treaty of Friendship between Great Britain and Nepal, 1923

populationTransfer.note: Britain recruited Nepali soldiers continuously from 1815; Gurkha regiments served in every major British campaign for 130 years and were split between the British and Indian armies in 1947.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Sugauli treaty line still defines Nepal's frontier, and the Kalapani dispute with India turns on which stream the treaty meant by the river Kali.
consequences.economicLegacy: Gurkha remittances and pensions have been a mainstay of the Nepali hill economy for two centuries, and the Rana regime survived on British goodwill bought with recruits.

peak.populationNote: Approximate: Nepal held no modern census before 1911 and early counts are unreliable.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Nepal’s largest recorded population: 5,600,000 people, counted in 1920.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: John Whelpton
evidence.work: A History of Nepal
evidence.supports: The Anglo-Nepalese War, the Rana regime and the 1923 treaty.

evidence.author: Kumar Pradhan
evidence.work: The Gorkha Conquests
evidence.supports: The making of the Gorkha state and the territories lost in 1816.

pedagogy.hook: Nepal was never colonised, and one reason is that the Company decided it was cheaper to hire Nepali soldiers than to fight them again.

misconception.belief: Britain conquered the whole of South Asia.
misconception.correction: Nepal, Bhutan and Afghanistan were never annexed. Nepal fought the Company to a standstill in the hills in 1814-16, gave up a third of its territory, and kept its independence, its own government and its own law. Britain got a Resident in Kathmandu, a recruiting ground, and a buffer against Tibet, and decided that was enough.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Nepal shows the limit of the empire's reach and the shape of its alternative: influence without administration, paid for in soldiers.

keyDates.what: The Anglo-Nepalese War begins; Nepal wins the first rounds
Treaty of Sugauli ratified; a third of Nepal ceded
The Kot massacre brings the Ranas to power for a century
Britain formally recognises Nepal's independence

territories.name: Bhutan
territories.formalName: Bhutan under British subsidy and treaty

modernSuccessors.name: Bhutan
modernSuccessors.note: India replaced Britain as the power guiding Bhutan's external relations in 1949; that clause was dropped in the revised treaty of 2007.

geoCoverage.label: A protected kingdom that kept its government
geoCoverage.change: The Treaty of Sinchula ended the Duar War: Bhutan gave up the fertile Duars along its southern edge and took an annual British subsidy in exchange.

acquisitions.how: Britain annexed the Duars by proclamation in November 1864, lost the fort at Dewangiri and retook it, and Bhutan signed the seizure into a treaty at Sinchula eleven months later, taking an annual subsidy of 50,000 rupees for its best farmland.

counterparties.name: The Druk Desi Tsultrim Namgyel and the Penlops of Trongsa and Paro
counterparties.lost: The Duars, some 2,000 square miles of the lowlands where its winter grazing and much of its revenue lay. The subsidy never matched their value.

acquisitions.how: Britain doubled the subsidy and Bhutan agreed to be guided by Britain in its external relations, while Britain undertook not to interfere in its internal administration at all.

counterparties.name: Ugyen Wangchuck, first King of Bhutan
counterparties.lost: Independent foreign policy. He gained British recognition, money and backing for the monarchy he had founded in 1907.

people.name: Ugyen Wangchuck
people.role: first Druk Gyalpo; had helped the British mission to Lhasa in 1904 and was rewarded with recognition

people.name: Charles Bell
people.role: British Political Officer in Sikkim who negotiated the treaty

statusPeriods.label: A subsidised neighbour
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Bhutan governed itself; Britain paid an annual subsidy for the Duars and dealt with whichever faction was winning the country's internal power struggles.

statusPeriods.label: Guided in external relations only
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain guided Bhutan's foreign relations and paid a subsidy; there was no Resident in the capital, no British court, no British troops and no British official in the internal administration.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Punakha, with contact through the Political Officer in Sikkim
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Bhutan was an absolute monarchy from 1907 and moved to a constitutional one only in 2008.

departures.how: Bhutan had never been British territory, so nothing was handed over: the Punakha treaty of 1910 lapsed with the transfer of power in Delhi, and Bhutan then negotiated its own treaty with independent India at Darjeeling in August 1949, which raised the subsidy and returned the enclave of Dewangiri.

led.name: Jigme Wangchuck
led.role: second Druk Gyalpo, who kept Bhutan out of both the Indian Empire and its dissolution

led.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
led.role: insisted on treating Bhutan as a sovereign neighbour rather than a princely state to be merged

departures.movement: The Bhutanese monarchy

cost.note: Nobody died. Bhutan is the only country in the region whose transition out of the British system involved no violence, no partition and no change of ruler.

departures.borders: The Duars stayed in India, and the boundary Britain drew in 1865 is still the India-Bhutan border; Bhutan's northern border with China has never been agreed.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Duars were turned into tea gardens under British and then Indian ownership, and the subsidy Bhutan received in exchange became the basis of its state finances into the twentieth century.
consequences.borderLegacy: Bhutan's southern border is the 1865 treaty line; its northern one, never settled with Tibet or China, produced the Doklam standoff between India and China in 2017.

peak.populationNote: Estimate only. Bhutan held no census before 1969, and colonial-era figures for it were guesses.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Bhutan’s largest recorded population: 700,000 people, counted in 1947.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Michael Aris
evidence.work: The Raven Crown: The Origins of Buddhist Monarchy in Bhutan
evidence.supports: The founding of the Wangchuck monarchy and its relations with British India.

pedagogy.hook: Britain never put a single official inside Bhutan; it paid the king a subsidy, took his best farmland, and left the rest alone.

misconception.belief: Every state with a British treaty was effectively a colony.
misconception.correction: Bhutan's 1910 treaty gave Britain a say in foreign relations and explicitly nothing else: no Resident in the capital, no British law, no garrison, no revenue. That is why Bhutan is a sovereign state today and Hyderabad, which had far more power on paper, is not.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Bhutan is the control case for the whole atlas: the least intrusive form of British influence, and the one place in South Asia where it left almost no institutional trace.

keyDates.what: Treaty of Sinchula: the Duars ceded for a subsidy
Ugyen Wangchuck crowned as Bhutan's first hereditary king
Treaty of Punakha: British guidance in foreign affairs only
India replaces Britain as treaty partner

territories.name: Afghanistan
territories.formalName: The Emirate of Afghanistan under British control of foreign relations

modernSuccessors.name: Afghanistan
modernSuccessors.note: The Treaty of Rawalpindi ended British control of Afghan foreign policy. Afghanistan celebrates 19 August as its independence day.

geoCoverage.label: A buffer state with no foreign policy
geoCoverage.change: After the Second Anglo-Afghan War, Britain took over Afghanistan's dealings with the outside world and paid its Amir a subsidy, while never governing an acre of it.

acquisitions.how: In the middle of the Second Anglo-Afghan War, Britain made Amir Yaqub Khan surrender his foreign relations, accept a British envoy at Kabul and cede the Khyber, Michni, Pishin and Sibi districts.

counterparties.name: The Emirate of Afghanistan
counterparties.lost: Control of its foreign policy, the passes into India, and the districts that became British Balochistan and part of the North-West Frontier Province.

counterparties.name: Yaqub Khan
counterparties.lost: His throne. Four months after signing, the British envoy was killed in Kabul, Britain reinvaded, and Yaqub Khan abdicated and was deported to India.

people.name: Abdur Rahman Khan
people.role: the Iron Amir, installed in 1880, who accepted British control of foreign policy and total freedom inside

people.name: Ayub Khan
people.role: destroyed a British brigade at Maiwand on 27 July 1880, the worst British defeat of the war

people.name: Frederick Roberts
people.role: British commander who occupied Kabul, hanged suspects after the envoy's death, and marched to Kandahar

cost.note: Deaths in the Second Anglo-Afghan War of 1878-80 on all sides, including disease and Afghan civilian deaths, which were not counted. The First Anglo-Afghan War of 1839-42 had cost more.

acquisitions.resistance: The war Britain thought it had won at Gandamak restarted at once: the mission at Kabul was destroyed in September 1879, and Ayub Khan wiped out a brigade at Maiwand in July 1880.

statusPeriods.label: Foreign policy in Calcutta, everything else in Kabul
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain paid the Amir an annual subsidy and arms, and in exchange he dealt with no other power; there was no British Resident in Kabul after 1879, no garrison and no administration.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kabul, with British control of external relations exercised from Calcutta
statusPeriods.franchise: None. Abdur Rahman used the subsidy and the guns to break the internal opposition, including the forced deportation of the Ghilzai and the conquest of the Hazarajat and Kafiristan in the 1890s.
statusPeriods.note: Britain fought three wars here in eighty years and never annexed a square mile of it: 1839-42, 1878-80 and 1919.

departures.how: Amanullah Khan declared full independence and attacked across the frontier; after a month of fighting, aerial bombing of Kabul and Jalalabad, and a stalemate, Britain conceded control of Afghan foreign relations at Rawalpindi.

led.name: Amanullah Khan
led.role: Amir who declared independence in 1919 and then tried to modernise the country; overthrown in 1929

led.name: Nadir Khan
led.role: Afghan commander who took Thal in the 1919 campaign and later became king

led.name: Charles Monro
led.role: British Commander-in-Chief in India, whose army was exhausted and mutinous after the world war

departures.movement: The Afghan monarchy and the Young Afghan reformers

cost.note: British Indian and Afghan battle deaths in the short Third Anglo-Afghan War of May to August 1919; British Indian losses to cholera in the campaign were higher than to fighting.

departures.borders: Rawalpindi gave Afghanistan its foreign policy but reaffirmed the Durand Line, which Afghanistan has never accepted; the argument over it outlived the British Empire and is still live between Kabul and Islamabad.

contested.note: Whether Afghanistan was ever a British protectorate at all is disputed. Britain controlled its foreign relations from 1879 to 1919 but never governed it, and Afghan historiography treats the country as continuously independent.

violence.note: The retreat from Kabul in January 1842 destroyed a column of about 16,500 soldiers and camp followers; almost all died in the passes or were taken captive.

toll.note: The 1842 retreat from Kabul. British accounts made much of a single European survivor reaching Jalalabad, but several hundred sepoys, women and children survived as captives or stragglers.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Durand Line of 1893 divides Pashtuns between Afghanistan and Pakistan and has never been accepted in Kabul; no border Britain drew in Asia has kept more people at war with the state that inherited it.
consequences.economicLegacy: British subsidies and arms let Abdur Rahman build the first centralised Afghan state, conquering the Hazarajat and Kafiristan; the state that resulted was funded from outside and has been ever since.

peak.populationNote: Estimate only; Afghanistan had no census in this period and colonial figures were guesses.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Afghanistan’s largest recorded population: 6,000,000 people, counted in 1919.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: William Dalrymple
evidence.work: Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan
evidence.supports: The First Anglo-Afghan War and the 1842 retreat, using Afghan as well as British sources.

evidence.author: Thomas Barfield
evidence.work: Afghanistan: A Cultural and Political History
evidence.supports: The making of the Afghan state under Abdur Rahman and the meaning of the buffer arrangement.

contested.note: Historians disagree about whether Afghanistan should be shown on a map of the British Empire at all. Britain controlled its foreign relations for forty years and paid its ruler, but never administered it, and Afghans do not regard the country as having been colonised.

pedagogy.hook: Britain fought three wars in Afghanistan in eighty years, lost an entire army in the passes in 1842, and never governed a single Afghan village.

misconception.belief: The British Empire took whatever it wanted.
misconception.correction: Afghanistan was invaded in 1839, in 1878 and defended against in 1919, and was never annexed. Britain settled for controlling its foreign policy from a distance, because occupying it had already cost an army. Colour it differently on the map: influence is not the same as rule, and the difference is exactly what students should learn to see.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Afghanistan defines the outer edge of the empire in Asia, and the Durand Line it left behind is still one of the world's most contested borders.

keyDates.what: The retreat from Kabul destroys a column of about 16,500
Gandamak: Britain takes Afghan foreign policy and the passes
The Durand Line divides Pashtun country
Treaty of Rawalpindi: Afghanistan regains its foreign policy

territories.name: French India under British occupation
territories.formalName: Pondicherry and the French settlements, captured and returned

modernSuccessors.name: India
modernSuccessors.note: France transferred the settlements de facto in 1954 and by treaty in 1962. They are now the Union Territory of Puducherry.

geoCoverage.label: Pondicherry razed
geoCoverage.change: The Company took Pondicherry after an eight-month siege and demolished its fortifications, ending French power in India. It was handed back at the Peace of Paris two years later.

geoCoverage.label: Held through the Napoleonic wars
geoCoverage.change: Taken again when revolutionary France went to war, and kept for twenty-three years. Britain returned the settlements after Waterloo, having decided that a French enclave with no army was harmless.

acquisitions.how: Eyre Coote besieged Pondicherry for eight months and starved it out; the Company then demolished the town's fortifications to make sure it could never again be a base.

counterparties.name: The French East India Company
counterparties.lost: Its capital in India and its position as Britain's rival for the subcontinent. Dupleix's strategy of ruling through Indian client princes had been the model the English then copied.

counterparties.name: The inhabitants of Pondicherry
counterparties.lost: Their town, whose walls and public buildings were levelled and whose people were displaced during a siege that ended in famine.

people.name: Eyre Coote
people.role: commanded the siege, having beaten the French at Wandiwash in 1760

people.name: Thomas Arthur, comte de Lally
people.role: French commander who surrendered Pondicherry and was executed in Paris for it in 1766

acquisitions.how: As soon as revolutionary France declared war, the Company took the French settlements again, and held them until the peace settlement after Waterloo returned them in 1816.

counterparties.name: The French Republic
counterparties.lost: Its Indian settlements for twenty-three years, and any prospect of using them as a base. Napoleon's plan to reach India ended in Egypt.

statusPeriods.label: Captured, demolished, returned
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Company held the ruins under military administration until the Peace of Paris handed them back with the fortifications gone.

statusPeriods.label: Held for twenty-three years
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The settlements were run from Madras as occupied territory, their French inhabitants left in place, until the post-Napoleonic settlement returned them.
statusPeriods.gapReason: Pondicherry was French again between 1763 and 1793, with a further short British occupation in 1778-1783 that is folded into this record rather than given its own period.

departures.how: Britain handed Pondicherry, Karaikal, Yanaon, Mahe and Chandernagore back to France under the 1814 Treaty of Paris, on terms that barred France from fortifying them or keeping troops there.

led.name: Joseph Francois Dupleix
led.role: the French governor whose earlier strategy of allying with Indian claimants taught the English how to conquer India

led.name: Robert Clive
led.role: made his reputation against the French in the Carnatic wars before Plassey

departures.movement: None; this was a settlement between two European states

cost.note: The Carnatic wars of 1746-63 killed thousands of Indian soldiers in the French and the English companies' armies and devastated the Coromandel countryside; no one counted them, because both companies counted only Europeans.

departures.borders: Five specks of French territory survived inside British India for another 138 years, which is why Sri Aurobindo could take refuge in Pondicherry in 1910 beyond the reach of British police.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris, 1814
instrument.note: The actual handover of Pondicherry took place on 4 December 1816.

consequences.borderLegacy: French Pondicherry and Portuguese Goa remained non-British enclaves in India until 1954 and 1961, and both became sanctuaries for Indian nationalists the British police could not touch.
consequences.economicLegacy: The Carnatic wars taught both companies that Indian land revenue could pay for European-officered armies. Britain acted on the lesson; France was left without a base from which to.

peak.populationNote: Approximate figure for all five French settlements at the return in 1816; contemporary counts were partial.

evidence.author: P. J. Marshall
evidence.work: The Making and Unmaking of Empires: Britain, India, and America c.1750-1783
evidence.supports: The Anglo-French struggle in India and its place in the wider imperial contest.

pedagogy.hook: Britain captured Pondicherry three times and gave it back three times; France still held it in 1947, and Indian revolutionaries hid there from British police.

misconception.belief: India was British and that was that.
misconception.correction: France held five small settlements in India until 1954 and Portugal held Goa, Daman and Diu until 1961. They mattered out of all proportion to their size: Sri Aurobindo escaped to Pondicherry in 1910, and the printing presses and political exiles of both enclaves were beyond the reach of British law.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Anglo-French wars in the Carnatic are where the East India Company learned to fight with Indian troops paid for by Indian revenue, which is the mechanism that took the subcontinent.

keyDates.what: The French take Madras; the Carnatic wars begin
Wandiwash: Coote defeats Lally and French power collapses
Pondicherry falls and is demolished
The settlements returned to France, unfortified

territories.name: Goa under British garrison
territories.formalName: Portuguese Goa, garrisoned by British troops 1799-1813

modernSuccessors.name: India
modernSuccessors.note: Portugal held Goa for 451 years. India annexed it by military action in December 1961, fourteen years after its own independence.

geoCoverage.label: An allied port under British troops
geoCoverage.change: British and Company troops garrisoned Goa's forts under an agreement with Portugal, Britain's oldest ally, to keep the harbour out of French hands during the Napoleonic wars.

acquisitions.how: Fearing a French descent on the Konkan while Tipu Sultan was still fighting, Britain landed troops in Goa with Portuguese consent and held the harbour forts for fourteen years.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Portugal
counterparties.lost: Effective control of its own colony's defences, conceded to an ally it could not refuse. Portuguese civil administration continued throughout.

counterparties.name: The people of Goa
counterparties.lost: Nothing changed in law; they got a foreign garrison and the trade disruption that came with the blockade of French and Dutch shipping.

contested.note: The dates of the British garrison are given variously as 1799 to 1813 and 1802 to 1813 in different accounts, and the arrangement was never formalised in a single published treaty. It was an alliance measure, not an annexation.

statusPeriods.label: Allied occupation of a neutral ally's port
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British troops held the forts and the harbour while Portuguese officials went on governing; sovereignty never changed hands and no British law was applied.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Not a full occupation: Britain held the defences of an allied colony whose own government continued to administer it, so control was partial rather than complete.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Panjim, under Portuguese administration, with British military command of the forts

departures.how: With Napoleon beaten in Russia and the Indian Ocean secure, Britain withdrew its garrison and handed the forts back to Portugal, which kept Goa for another 148 years.

led.name: Marquess Wellesley
led.role: Governor-General who ordered the occupation as part of the campaign against French influence in India

departures.movement: None; a wartime arrangement between allied governments

cost.note: No fighting and no recorded deaths beyond the usual garrison losses to fever. This was an occupation by agreement, not by force.

departures.borders: Nothing was redrawn. Goa stayed Portuguese until Indian troops entered it in December 1961, in an operation Portugal called an invasion and India called liberation.

consequences.borderLegacy: Portugal's continued possession of Goa left independent India with a colonial enclave on its west coast until 1961, and the annexation was condemned by Britain and the United States at the United Nations.

peak.populationNote: Approximate. Portuguese Goa's population in the early nineteenth century is known only from partial parish and revenue returns.

evidence.author: Malyn Newitt
evidence.work: A History of Portuguese Overseas Expansion 1400-1668
evidence.supports: Portuguese Goa's institutions and its position relative to the other European powers in India.

contested.note: This is the least certain record in the shard. The garrison's dates, its legal basis and whether it should count as British control at all are all arguable; it is included because leaving it out would make the map imply Goa was untouched, and because it shows what an alliance occupation looked like.

pedagogy.hook: Britain quietly garrisoned Portuguese Goa for fourteen years to keep the French out, then handed it back and let Portugal keep it until 1961.

misconception.belief: European colonies in India all ended in 1947.
misconception.correction: Portugal held Goa, Daman and Diu until Indian troops took them in December 1961, and France handed over Pondicherry only in 1954. Britain's departure in 1947 did not end European rule in India; it ended British rule, and the last European colony there outlasted it by fourteen years.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the empire acting as an alliance system rather than an owner: sometimes British troops held a place they had no intention of keeping.

keyDates.what: British troops garrison Goa's forts with Portuguese consent
The garrison withdraws; Portugal resumes full control
India annexes Goa after 451 years of Portuguese rule

events.title: Plassey
events.summary: Robert Clive's 3,000 men beat the Nawab of Bengal's 50,000 in a few hours, because the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar had been bought beforehand and kept most of the army standing still. Around twenty-two of Clive's men were killed.
events.significance: It made the East India Company the power behind the throne in the richest province of Asia, and it did so by conspiracy: the Jagat Seth bankers financed it, Mir Jafar sold the battle, and Clive took a personal fortune out of the Bengal treasury.

places.name: Palashi (Plassey)
places.note: A mango grove on the Bhagirathi, north of Calcutta.

places.name: Murshidabad
places.note: The Nawab's capital, then one of the richest cities in the world.

people.name: Robert Clive
people.role: Company commander who arranged the conspiracy and won the battle

people.name: Siraj-ud-Daula
people.role: Nawab of Bengal, aged 23; fled the field, was captured and killed within a fortnight

people.name: Mir Jafar
people.role: Bengali commander who agreed in advance not to fight and was made Nawab as his reward

people.name: Mir Madan
people.role: artillery commander loyal to the Nawab, killed by a cannonball early in the fighting

people.name: Jagat Seth Mahtab Rai
people.role: banker whose house financed the plot and guaranteed the payments to Mir Jafar

toll.note: About 500 of the Nawab's men and roughly 22 of the Company's were killed, on Company returns. The battle was decided by an agreement, not by casualties.

pedagogy.hook: The battle that began the British conquest of India was fixed in advance, and about twenty-two men on the winning side died.

misconception.belief: Britain conquered India through superior weapons and discipline.
misconception.correction: At Plassey the decisive factor was money: Bengali bankers and a general bought off in advance. The Company's power in India rested from the start on Indian capital, Indian soldiers and Indian collaborators under pressure. It won the shooting battles later, with sepoys paid out of Bengali taxes.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Plassey is the moment a trading company became a kingmaker, and the model it used, buy the succession and bill the province, was repeated across India for the next sixty years.

evidence.author: William Dalrymple
evidence.work: The Anarchy: The Relentless Rise of the East India Company
evidence.supports: The conspiracy, the bankers and the course of the battle.

contested.note: Historians differ on how far Plassey was decisive at all: some treat Buxar in 1764 as the real conquest, since Plassey only installed a client Nawab while Buxar beat three armies in the field.

events.title: Buxar
events.summary: Hector Munro's Company army of about 7,000 destroyed the combined forces of the Nawab of Bengal, the Nawab of Awadh and the Mughal emperor, perhaps 40,000 men, in a single morning at Buxar on the Ganges.
events.significance: Buxar, not Plassey, is where the Company won northern India in open battle. Ten months later the defeated emperor signed over the diwani of Bengal, and a trading company became the government of twenty million people.

places.name: Buxar
places.note: On the south bank of the Ganges in modern Bihar.

people.name: Mir Qasim
people.role: Nawab of Bengal who had tried to govern independently, abolished internal duties to break the Company's trading privilege, and lost his state for it

people.name: Shuja-ud-Daula
people.role: Nawab of Awadh, who bought his throne back after the defeat for five million rupees

people.name: Shah Alam II
people.role: Mughal emperor, present at the battle, who changed sides afterwards and granted the Company the diwani

people.name: Hector Munro
people.role: Company commander; had earlier blown mutinous sepoys from cannon to restore discipline

toll.note: Company returns give about 850 of their own killed and wounded and estimate allied losses at several thousand. The higher figures come from the pursuit, which was not counted.

pedagogy.hook: Three Indian rulers, including the Mughal emperor, fought the East India Company together and lost in one morning.

misconception.belief: Indian rulers did not resist the Company seriously.
misconception.correction: Mir Qasim abolished the internal trade duties that gave Company men an unfair advantage over Indian merchants, built a modern army, and formed a coalition with Awadh and the emperor. He lost, and the loss is what made the conquest possible. Resistance was real, organised and defeated.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is the battle that gave the Company the revenue of Bengal by right of conquest, dressed as a legal grant from the emperor it had just beaten.

evidence.author: P. J. Marshall
evidence.work: Bengal: The British Bridgehead, Eastern India 1740-1828
evidence.supports: The war with Mir Qasim, Buxar and the settlement that followed.

events.title: The Bengal famine of 1770
events.summary: After a failed monsoon in 1768 and a worse one in 1769, famine killed a large part of Bengal's population while the East India Company went on collecting the land revenue and its servants traded privately in grain.
events.significance: The first famine under British administration, five years after the Company took the diwani. Revenue collection actually rose during it. News of it in Britain helped force the Regulating Act of 1773 and the first parliamentary control over the Company.

places.name: Murshidabad
places.note: The Nawab's capital, at the centre of the worst-hit districts.

people.name: Warren Hastings
people.role: Governor of Bengal from 1772, who reported that revenue had been 'violently kept up' through the famine year

people.name: Muhammad Reza Khan
people.role: the Company's Indian deputy in charge of revenue collection, later prosecuted and acquitted over the famine

toll.note: Contemporary Company estimates spoke of a third of Bengal dying, which would be around ten million. Modern historians argue for lower figures, and some for far lower. There was no census, and the estimates were made by people with an interest in the answer.
toll.source: East India Company servants' contemporary estimates for the one-third figure; Rajat Datta, Society, Economy and the Market (2000), for the lower modern reconstructions. There was no census.

pedagogy.hook: In the worst famine year, the Company's revenue collection from Bengal went up.

misconception.belief: Famines are natural disasters that governments can only respond to.
misconception.correction: The monsoon failed, but what turned shortage into mass death was policy: a revenue demand kept up through the crisis, private grain trading by Company servants, and no relief system at all. Amartya Sen's later work on entitlements shows famines are usually about who can afford food, not whether food exists.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the first entry in a ledger that runs through 1876, 1899 and 1943, and it set the pattern: the harvest fails, the demand does not, and nobody in charge is accountable.

evidence.author: Rajat Datta
evidence.work: Society, Economy and the Market: Commercialization in Rural Bengal c.1760-1800
evidence.supports: Grain markets, revenue collection and the scale of the 1770 mortality.

evidence.author: Amartya Sen
evidence.work: Poverty and Famines: An Essay on Entitlement and Deprivation
evidence.supports: The analytical point that famine deaths follow the collapse of entitlements, not simply of supply.

contested.note: The death toll is one of the most disputed numbers in Indian history. The traditional figure of ten million, a third of Bengal, comes from Company estimates; recent work argues for substantially lower totals. No count was made and none can now be made.

events.title: Parliament takes hold of the Company
events.summary: The Regulating Act of 1773 created a Governor-General and a Supreme Court at Calcutta and put the Company under parliamentary scrutiny; Pitt's India Act of 1784 added a government Board of Control with the final say over everything except patronage.
events.significance: Britain decided that a company governing millions of people could not be left to its shareholders, but stopped short of taking over. For seventy-four more years India was ruled by a company supervised by a cabinet minister, which suited both.

places.name: Leadenhall Street, London
places.note: East India House, the Company's headquarters.

places.name: Westminster
places.note: Where the Company's government was debated and, in Hastings's case, put on trial.

people.name: Warren Hastings
people.role: first Governor-General; impeached in 1788 and acquitted in 1795 after a seven-year trial on charges of corruption and cruelty in Bengal

people.name: Edmund Burke
people.role: led the impeachment, arguing that arbitrary power over Indians was as intolerable as arbitrary power over Britons

people.name: William Pitt the Younger
people.role: Prime Minister whose 1784 Act created the Board of Control

people.name: Philip Francis
people.role: councillor who fought Hastings politically and in a duel, and supplied Burke with his material

pedagogy.hook: For seven years the British Parliament put a former Governor-General on trial for what he had done in India, and then acquitted him.

misconception.belief: Nobody at the time thought there was anything wrong with the way India was governed.
misconception.correction: The Hastings impeachment ran from 1788 to 1795 in Westminster Hall, with Burke arguing that British power in India was lawless. Nabobs returning with Indian fortunes were a scandal in British politics for a generation. The argument was lost, but it was had, loudly and in public.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It set the constitutional shape of British India for seventy years: a company that governed, a minister who answered for it, and an arrangement in which responsibility could always be passed on.

evidence.author: Nicholas B. Dirks
evidence.work: The Scandal of Empire: India and the Creation of Imperial Britain
evidence.supports: The impeachment, the politics of the nabobs and the reform of Company government.

events.title: The Anglo-Mysore Wars
events.summary: Four wars in thirty-two years between the Company and Mysore under Haidar Ali and his son Tipu Sultan. Mysore won the first two, including a British surrender at Pollilur in 1780; the last ended with Tipu killed defending Seringapatam.
events.significance: Mysore was the strongest opponent the Company ever faced in India: it had rocket artillery, a modern-drilled army and French allies. Beating it took four wars, three alliances and thirty years, and its defeat opened the whole south.

places.name: Srirangapatna (Seringapatam)
places.note: Tipu's island capital, stormed on 4 May 1799.

places.name: Pollilur
places.note: Where Mysorean forces destroyed a British detachment in September 1780.

people.name: Haidar Ali
people.role: soldier who took power in Mysore in 1761 and beat the Company twice

people.name: Tipu Sultan
people.role: his son; built a navy and a rocket corps, sought French, Ottoman and Afghan alliances, and died at the breach in 1799

people.name: Charles Cornwallis
people.role: Governor-General who took half of Mysore in 1792 and held Tipu's sons as hostages

people.name: Arthur Wellesley
people.role: commanded a division at the final siege; later Duke of Wellington

toll.note: Deaths across four wars on all sides, including the famine and devastation of the Carnatic in 1780-84. No systematic count exists; the range is a scholarly estimate.

pedagogy.hook: Mysore's rocket artillery so impressed the British that they took captured rockets home, and the Congreve rocket used against the Americans in 1814 was the result.

misconception.belief: Indian states fought with obsolete weapons against modern European armies.
misconception.correction: Mysore under Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan had iron-cased rockets, French-trained infantry, its own naval programme and diplomatic missions to Paris, Istanbul and Kabul. It beat British armies in 1780 and forced a negotiated peace in 1784. The Company won in the end by weight of alliances, revenue and numbers.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Mysore is the counter-example to the idea that Indian defeat was inevitable, and its four wars show how the Company actually expanded: by assembling coalitions of Indian states against one Indian state at a time.

evidence.author: Kate Brittlebank
evidence.work: Tipu Sultan's Search for Legitimacy: Islam and Kingship in a Hindu Domain
evidence.supports: Tipu's state, his army and the British representation of him.

events.title: The end of the Maratha empire
events.summary: The Company put 120,000 troops into the field, the largest force it had ever assembled, broke the Pindari bands and the armies of the Peshwa, Scindia, Holkar and Bhonsle, and abolished the office of Peshwa altogether.
events.significance: After 1818 no Indian power could challenge the Company in the field. The states that survived did so as protected princely states, which is why two fifths of India was still ruled by Indian princes in 1947 rather than by the Crown.

places.name: Koregaon Bhima
places.note: Where a Company force including Mahar soldiers held off a much larger Peshwa army on 1 January 1818; the pillar there is now a Dalit memorial.

places.name: Poona
places.note: The Peshwa's capital, taken in November 1817.

people.name: Baji Rao II
people.role: last Peshwa; surrendered in June 1818 and was pensioned to Bithur near Kanpur

people.name: Francis Rawdon-Hastings
people.role: Governor-General who planned the campaign against the Pindaris and then the Marathas

people.name: Mountstuart Elphinstone
people.role: Resident at Poona; took over the government of the conquered Deccan

people.name: Malhar Rao Holkar III
people.role: ruler of Indore, defeated at Mahidpur in December 1817

toll.note: Combined losses across the Pindari and Maratha campaigns, including irregulars and civilians in the country swept by the Company's columns and by the Pindari bands. Only British and Company casualties were counted.

pedagogy.hook: The largest army the East India Company ever assembled, 120,000 men, was raised to hunt down mounted raiders and ended by abolishing the Maratha empire.

misconception.belief: The princely states were leftovers Britain had not got round to conquering.
misconception.correction: They were made deliberately in 1817-18. Britain preferred treaties to administration: a defeated ruler who kept his throne cost nothing to govern and could be relied on to keep his own subjects quiet. The princely map of 1947 is the direct output of this campaign.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is the moment the shape of the Indian Empire was set, half provinces and half princely states, and it explains why 1947 needed 565 separate accessions.

evidence.author: Stewart Gordon
evidence.work: The Marathas 1600-1818
evidence.supports: The Maratha state and its defeat.

events.title: The Anglo-Nepalese War
events.summary: Two years of fighting in the Himalayan foothills, in which Nepali forces destroyed British columns at Nalapani and Jaithak before superior numbers told. Nepal kept its independence and lost about a third of its territory.
events.significance: It fixed Nepal's borders, gave Britain the Himalayan hill stations from Simla to Darjeeling, and started Gurkha recruitment: the British Indian Army took its enemies of 1815 into its own ranks and kept them for 130 years.

places.name: Nalapani (Kalanga)
places.note: Where about 600 Nepali defenders held out against 3,000 British troops for a month in 1814.

people.name: Balbhadra Kunwar
people.role: commanded the defence of Nalapani and walked out through the British lines with his surviving men

people.name: Amar Singh Thapa
people.role: commander in the western hills whose resistance impressed the British into recruiting Gurkhas

people.name: David Ochterlony
people.role: British commander who won the war by patience and numbers, and became the first Resident at Kathmandu

toll.note: Deaths on all sides over two years, mostly from disease and mountain campaigning. Neither side counted the other's losses.

pedagogy.hook: The British were so impressed by the soldiers who beat them at Nalapani that they started recruiting them, and Gurkha regiments have served in the British army ever since.

misconception.belief: Colonial armies were made up of British soldiers.
misconception.correction: The Indian Army was overwhelmingly Indian and Nepali: about 1.4 million served in the First World War and 2.5 million volunteered in the Second, the largest volunteer army in history. British officers commanded, but the empire in Asia was held, and extended, by soldiers recruited from the places it had conquered.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains both Nepal's survival as an independent country and the shape of the army that conquered and held the rest of the empire.

evidence.author: John Whelpton
evidence.work: A History of Nepal
evidence.supports: The war, the Treaty of Sugauli and the beginning of Gurkha recruitment.

events.title: The First Anglo-Burmese War
events.summary: A border quarrel in Arakan grew into a two-year war in which disease killed most of the 15,000 British and Indian dead. Burma gave up Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim and paid an indemnity of a million pounds.
events.significance: It cost the Company about 13 million pounds, nearly bankrupted it, and brought the whole of the north-east into British India. It also broke the Konbaung kingdom's finances and set up the two further wars that ended Burmese independence.

places.name: Yandabo
places.note: Village on the Irrawaddy where the treaty was signed, sixty kilometres from the Burmese capital.

places.name: Rangoon
places.note: Occupied by the British expedition in May 1824.

people.name: Maha Bandula
people.role: Burmese commander-in-chief, killed by a mortar shell at Danubyu in April 1825

people.name: Archibald Campbell
people.role: British commander of the Rangoon expedition

people.name: Gambhir Singh
people.role: Manipuri prince who raised a levy, fought alongside the British and recovered his throne

toll.money: About 13 million pounds sterling to the East India Company, and an indemnity of one million pounds from Burma.
toll.note: British and Indian deaths were about 15,000, the great majority from disease. Burmese military and civilian deaths were never counted.

pedagogy.hook: The war that gave Britain Assam killed about fifteen thousand of its own soldiers, and most of them died of disease rather than in battle.

misconception.belief: Colonial wars were cheap and easy for Britain.
misconception.correction: The First Anglo-Burmese War cost 13 million pounds, more than the East India Company earned from Bengal in a year, and nearly forced it into bankruptcy. Cholera, dysentery and malaria killed far more of its soldiers than the Burmese army did. Expansion often looked reckless even to the people paying for it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It brought Assam, Manipur and the Burmese coast into British India in one treaty, and its expense is one reason Parliament ended the Company's trading monopoly in 1833.

evidence.author: Thant Myint-U
evidence.work: The Making of Modern Burma
evidence.supports: The Konbaung state, the war and the Treaty of Yandabo.

events.title: The retreat from Kabul
events.summary: Britain invaded Afghanistan to replace Dost Mohammad Khan with a client, occupied Kabul for two years, and then lost almost an entire column of about 16,500 soldiers and camp followers in the passes on the retreat in January 1842.
events.significance: The worst British military disaster in Asia in the nineteenth century. It established Afghanistan as the limit of British power, and taught the Government of India to prefer buying Afghan rulers to occupying their country.

places.name: Kabul
places.note: Occupied 1839-42.

places.name: Gandamak
places.note: Where the last organised remnant of the retreating column was destroyed on 13 January 1842.

people.name: Dost Mohammad Khan
people.role: Amir deposed by the invasion and restored by the British in 1843, after they had spent two years and thousands of lives removing him

people.name: Wazir Akbar Khan
people.role: his son; led the rising in Kabul in November 1841

people.name: Shah Shuja
people.role: the British client placed on the throne, assassinated in April 1842

people.name: William Brydon
people.role: army surgeon whose arrival at Jalalabad became the emblem of the disaster, though he was not the only survivor

toll.note: The column that left Kabul on 6 January 1842 numbered about 4,500 soldiers and 12,000 camp followers. Almost all died or were taken captive. Afghan losses over the whole war were never counted.

pedagogy.hook: Of a column of about 16,500 people that left Kabul in January 1842, the story goes that one man reached safety; in fact a few hundred survived as captives, which is barely better.

misconception.belief: British expansion was a steady advance that only ever went forwards.
misconception.correction: Afghanistan defeated Britain in 1842 and again in 1919, and was never annexed. The 1842 invasion was undertaken on a false premise, that Dost Mohammad was about to ally with Russia. Britain removed him, lost an army, and then put him back on the throne in 1843.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the empire's most famous defeat in Asia, and it set the doctrine that governed the whole north-west frontier for the next century: buy the Amir, hold the passes, do not occupy the country.

evidence.author: William Dalrymple
evidence.work: Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan
evidence.supports: The invasion, the occupation and the retreat, using Afghan sources alongside British ones.

events.title: The Anglo-Sikh Wars
events.summary: Two wars against the Sikh empire of Ranjit Singh's successors, fought at Ferozeshah, Sobraon, Chillianwala and Gujrat. They were the bloodiest battles the Company fought in India, and at Chillianwala it came close to defeat.
events.significance: Annexing the Punjab in 1849 completed British control of the subcontinent up to the Afghan hills, delivered the recruiting ground that supplied half the Indian Army by 1914, and produced the province that partition would tear apart in 1947.

places.name: Chillianwala
places.note: Battle of 13 January 1849, so costly that Parliament debated whether it was a defeat.

places.name: Lahore
places.note: The Sikh capital, where the annexation was proclaimed.

people.name: Duleep Singh
people.role: maharaja, deposed at ten and later sent to England; the Koh-i-Noor was taken from his treasury

people.name: Rani Jind Kaur
people.role: regent, imprisoned and exiled for resisting; escaped to Nepal disguised as a servant

people.name: Sham Singh Attariwala
people.role: Sikh general who refused to retreat at Sobraon and was killed there in February 1846

people.name: Hugh Gough
people.role: British commander whose frontal attacks produced the casualty lists that shocked London

toll.note: Combined battle deaths across both wars. British and Company losses were counted precisely; Khalsa losses were estimated by the victors and are uncertain.

pedagogy.hook: The Koh-i-Noor diamond in the British crown jewels was taken from a ten-year-old boy as part of a war indemnity in 1849.

misconception.belief: The Sikh empire was a minor kingdom easily overrun.
misconception.correction: The Khalsa army was trained by European officers, had the best artillery in India, and at Chillianwala in January 1849 inflicted losses so heavy that the British commander was replaced before news of the next battle arrived. The Punjab was the last independent power in the subcontinent, and beating it took two wars in four years.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The annexation of 1849 produced the province that supplied the Indian Army, absorbed the canal colonies, and suffered the worst of partition ninety-eight years later.

evidence.author: Khushwant Singh
evidence.work: A History of the Sikhs, Volume 2: 1839-2004
evidence.supports: The Sikh state after Ranjit Singh, the two wars and the annexation.

events.title: The doctrine of lapse
events.summary: Dalhousie ruled that a dependent Indian state whose ruler died without a natural heir passed to the Company, refusing the adoptions that Hindu law allowed. Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Sambalpur and others were annexed on that basis, and Awadh for misgovernment.
events.significance: It told every ruler in India that no treaty and no custom protected them. Rulers dispossessed by lapse, or their heirs, led much of the fighting in 1857, and after the rebellion the Crown formally guaranteed adoptions to buy the princes back.

places.name: Jhansi
places.note: Annexed in 1853 when Lakshmibai's adopted son was refused recognition.

places.name: Lucknow
places.note: Capital of Awadh, annexed for misgovernment in February 1856.

people.name: James Broun-Ramsay, Lord Dalhousie
people.role: Governor-General 1848-56 who applied the doctrine and annexed eight states

people.name: Lakshmibai, Rani of Jhansi
people.role: widow whose adopted heir was refused in 1853; led the defence of Jhansi in 1858 and was killed near Gwalior

people.name: Nana Sahib
people.role: adopted son of the last Peshwa, whose pension was stopped on his father's death; led the rising at Kanpur

people.name: Wajid Ali Shah
people.role: King of Awadh, deposed in 1856 and exiled to Calcutta

pedagogy.hook: A rule about adoption cost eight Indian rulers their states in eight years, and two of the people it dispossessed led the rebellion of 1857.

misconception.belief: The 1857 rebellion came out of nowhere.
misconception.correction: Between 1848 and 1856 Britain annexed Satara, Jaitpur, Sambalpur, Jhansi, Nagpur and Awadh, stopped hereditary pensions, and told rulers their adopted heirs did not count. Nana Sahib lost a pension, Lakshmibai lost a kingdom, and the Bengal army lost the home province from which a third of it was recruited. The rebellion had a list of grievances with dates on them.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest example of policy causing rebellion, and of the empire learning from it: after 1858 Britain guaranteed the princes' adoptions and never annexed another state.

evidence.author: Barbara N. Ramusack
evidence.work: The Indian Princes and their States
evidence.supports: The doctrine of lapse, the annexations and the post-1858 guarantee of adoption.

contested.note: Some historians argue the doctrine was applied less systematically than nationalist accounts suggest, and that Dalhousie annexed where it was convenient rather than following a consistent rule. That the annexations happened, and their effect on 1857, is not disputed.

events.title: The rebellion of 1857
events.summary: Sepoys of the Bengal army mutinied at Meerut, marched on Delhi and proclaimed the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar their sovereign. Peasants, dispossessed landholders and rulers joined them across the north. It took Britain fourteen months and Indian troops to win.
events.significance: The largest armed challenge to British rule anywhere in the empire in the nineteenth century. It ended Company government, produced reprisals that scarred northern India, and made the British permanently distrustful of the people they ruled.

places.name: Meerut
places.note: Where the rising began on 10 May 1857.

places.name: Delhi
places.note: Seized by the rebels and retaken by assault in September 1857.

places.name: Kanpur (Cawnpore)
places.note: Site of the killing of British prisoners at Bibighar and of the reprisals that followed.

places.name: Lucknow
places.note: Besieged twice; Awadh fought on into 1859.

people.name: Bahadur Shah Zafar
people.role: last Mughal emperor, proclaimed leader by the rebels; tried and exiled to Rangoon, where he died

people.name: Lakshmibai, Rani of Jhansi
people.role: led the defence of Jhansi and was killed in action near Gwalior in June 1858

people.name: Begum Hazrat Mahal
people.role: held Lucknow and led Awadh's resistance; refused an amnesty and died in exile in Nepal

people.name: Mangal Pandey
people.role: sepoy at Barrackpore who attacked his officers in March 1857 and was hanged in April

people.name: Kunwar Singh
people.role: eighty-year-old landholder of Jagdishpur in Bihar who led a campaign across three provinces

people.name: John Nicholson
people.role: British commander at the assault on Delhi, killed in the breach

toll.note: About 6,000 Europeans died, from military and civil returns. Indian deaths were never counted and no register survives that could count them. The lower figure covers deaths in the fighting and in the hangings and village burnings that followed it; the upper is a reconstruction of excess mortality that adds the famine and epidemic disease that came with them, read out of the population shortfall in the North-Western Provinces returns of the 1860s. Both ends are estimates with wide margins, not counts.
toll.source: No count exists. The 800,000 end is an excess-mortality reconstruction from the North-Western Provinces population returns of the 1860s. The ten million often quoted is Amaresh Misra, War of Civilisations: India AD 1857 (2007), rejected by specialists; this atlas does not carry it.

pedagogy.hook: Whether you call 1857 a mutiny, a rebellion or the first war of independence tells people where your textbook was printed.

misconception.belief: 1857 was a mutiny by soldiers upset about greased cartridges.
misconception.correction: The cartridge rumour lit it. The fuel was a decade of annexations, land settlements that ruined landholders and cultivators, and the seizure of Awadh in 1856, home province of a third of the Bengal army. Civilians rose in Awadh and Bihar after the soldiers did, and kept fighting after the army had been beaten.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Everything students recognise as 'the Raj', the Viceroy, the durbars, the racial distance, begins here, and begins as a reaction to nearly losing control.

evidence.author: Rudrangshu Mukherjee
evidence.work: Awadh in Revolt 1857-1858: A Study of Popular Resistance
evidence.supports: The popular character of the rising in Awadh.

evidence.author: William Dalrymple
evidence.work: The Last Mughal: The Fall of a Dynasty, Delhi 1857
evidence.supports: Delhi in 1857, Bahadur Shah Zafar's position and the sack of the city.

evidence.author: Kim A. Wagner
evidence.work: The Great Fear of 1857: Rumours, Conspiracies and the Making of the Indian Uprising
evidence.supports: The character and scale of the violence and the reprisals, and the absence of any count of the Indian dead.

contested.note: The name, the causes and the death toll are all disputed. Indian historians from V. D. Savarkar in 1909 onward have called it the first war of independence; older British accounts called it the Mutiny; the number of Indian dead was never established and estimates differ by an order of magnitude.

events.title: The Crown takes India from the Company
events.summary: Parliament abolished the East India Company's government and transferred its territories, its treasury and its army — about 200,000 men, down from a peak near 280,000 once the mutinied Bengal regiments were disbanded — to the Crown. Victoria's proclamation was read at Allahabad on 1 November 1858.
events.significance: It ended 258 years of rule by a chartered company and created the Raj: a Secretary of State in the Cabinet, a Viceroy in Calcutta, and a guarantee to the princes that their adoptions would be recognised, so that no state would ever be annexed again.

places.name: Allahabad
places.note: Where the Queen's proclamation was read on 1 November 1858.

places.name: East India House, London
places.note: The Company's headquarters, sold and demolished in 1861.

people.name: Charles Canning
people.role: last Governor-General of the Company and first Viceroy; nicknamed 'Clemency' for restraining the reprisals

people.name: Victoria
people.role: Queen whose proclamation promised religious non-interference and equal admission to office regardless of race, a promise not kept

people.name: Benjamin Disraeli
people.role: drove the transfer through the Commons and later gave Victoria the title of Empress

pedagogy.hook: The British government did not conquer India in 1858; it took over from a company that had already done it, and paid the shareholders off until 1874.

misconception.belief: The British Empire in India was built by the British state.
misconception.correction: It was built by a joint-stock company with shareholders, a private army and a monopoly, and the state took it over only after the company's rule collapsed in rebellion. The Company itself was not wound up until 1874, and its shareholders were compensated out of Indian revenue.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the hinge of the whole Indian story, and it shows the direction of travel: the empire nationalised its conquest only after the conquest had failed to stay quiet.

evidence.author: Barbara D. Metcalf and Thomas R. Metcalf
evidence.work: A Concise History of Modern India
evidence.supports: The transfer of power and the shape of the government it created.

events.title: The conquest of Burma
events.summary: Two more wars finished what 1826 began. In 1852 a quarrel over harbour dues at Rangoon ended with Pegu annexed by proclamation; in 1885 a fine on a British timber company ended with an eleven-day war, the exile of King Thibaw and the abolition of the monarchy.
events.significance: Burma lost its coast, then its independence, then its king, and was attached to British India as a province. Putting down the guerrilla war in the countryside afterwards took five years and 30,000 troops, and the fighters were classified as bandits so they could be hanged.

places.name: Mandalay
places.note: The royal capital, taken on 28 November 1885.

places.name: Rangoon
places.note: The port whose harbour dues triggered the 1852 war.

people.name: Thibaw Min
people.role: last king of Burma, deported to Ratnagiri in India where he died in 1916

people.name: Supayalat
people.role: queen, exiled with him; allowed back to Burma only after his death

people.name: James Broun-Ramsay, Lord Dalhousie
people.role: Governor-General who annexed Pegu in 1852 without a treaty

people.name: Randolph Churchill
people.role: Secretary of State for India who ordered the 1885 invasion and timed the annexation for New Year's Day

toll.note: The wars themselves cost few British lives; the five-year campaign to break resistance in Upper Burma after 1886 cost far more Burmese ones, and they were recorded as dacoits killed rather than counted as war dead.

pedagogy.hook: Britain abolished the Burmese monarchy by proclamation on New Year's Day 1886, three weeks after taking the capital, and shipped the king to India by steamer.

misconception.belief: Colonial wars were declared for strategic reasons after careful deliberation.
misconception.correction: The 1852 war began with two sea captains complaining about harbour dues, and the 1885 war with a fine imposed on the Bombay Burmah Trading Corporation for underpaying timber royalties. Commercial grievances escalated by men on the spot produced two annexations and the end of a 1,000-year-old monarchy.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows conquest as a series of small commercial quarrels amplified by force, and it left Burma with no monarchy, no aristocracy and no state tradition to build on in 1948.

evidence.author: Michael W. Charney
evidence.work: A History of Modern Burma
evidence.supports: The second and third wars, the annexation and the five-year campaign against Burmese resistance that followed.

events.title: Victoria becomes Empress of India
events.summary: Disraeli's Royal Titles Act made Victoria Empress of India, and Lord Lytton proclaimed it at a durbar in Delhi on 1 January 1877 in front of the assembled princes, with banners, elephants and a specially composed heraldry.
events.significance: It invented a ceremonial language for the Raj: the princes were arranged in a hierarchy of gun salutes and given coats of arms, and were shown as feudal subordinates of a British empress rather than as allies with treaties.

places.name: Delhi durbar site, Coronation Park
places.note: The plain north of Delhi used for the durbars of 1877, 1903 and 1911.

people.name: Benjamin Disraeli
people.role: Prime Minister who devised the title, partly to match the emperors of Russia and Germany

people.name: Robert Bulwer-Lytton
people.role: Viceroy who staged the durbar, in the middle of a famine that would kill millions

people.name: Victoria
people.role: Queen-Empress, who never visited India

pedagogy.hook: The durbar that proclaimed Victoria Empress of India was held in January 1877, while famine was killing millions of her new subjects a few hundred miles south.

misconception.belief: The pageantry of the Raj reflected old Indian traditions Britain respected.
misconception.correction: Most of it was invented in the 1870s. The gun salutes, the order of precedence, the coats of arms and the durbar ritual were designed by British officials, drawing on Mughal forms but arranging Indian rulers into a British feudal hierarchy that had never existed. David Cannadine calls this 'ornamentalism': the empire re-imagined as a class system.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the empire building a story about itself, and it is worth asking who the pageantry was for: the princes, the Indian public, or the British newspapers.

evidence.author: David Cannadine
evidence.work: Ornamentalism: How the British Saw Their Empire
evidence.supports: The invention of imperial ceremonial and the ranking of Indian princes.

events.title: The Great Famine of 1876-78
events.summary: Drought across the Deccan and southern India coincided with record grain exports to Britain and a relief policy built on Richard Temple's ration of about one pound of rice a day for heavy labour, less than the Buchenwald ration of the 1940s.
events.significance: Between five and ten million people died. The scandal produced the Famine Commission of 1880 and the Famine Codes, the first systematic relief rules in India, and it also produced the nationalist argument that British rule was killing Indians by policy.

places.name: Madras
places.note: The presidency capital, where the government resisted London's demands to cut relief further.

places.name: Bellary
places.note: One of the worst-hit districts, where mortality in some talukas exceeded a quarter of the population.

people.name: Richard Temple
people.role: Famine Commissioner who cut the relief ration and imposed a distance test to deter applicants

people.name: Robert Bulwer-Lytton
people.role: Viceroy who insisted relief must not interfere with the grain market and held the imperial durbar in January 1877

people.name: William Digby
people.role: British journalist in Madras whose account of the famine and its official handling was published in 1878

people.name: Dadabhai Naoroji
people.role: used the famine in his drain-of-wealth argument that British rule was impoverishing India

toll.note: Estimates for southern and western India in 1876-78. Colonial mortality registration was incomplete and different baselines give different excess-death totals, which is why the range is so wide. It is one of the deadliest famines on record anywhere.
toll.source: Colonial mortality registration, which was incomplete; the excess-death reconstructions summarised in Mike Davis, Late Victorian Holocausts (2001), and the demographic work of Arup Maharatna.

pedagogy.hook: The relief ration set for famine labourers in 1877 provided fewer calories than the ration at Buchenwald.

misconception.belief: Famines happened because India could not grow enough food.
misconception.correction: India exported a record volume of grain during the famine years, and the railways that could have moved food inland were moving it to ports. Relief was deliberately made unpleasant so that only the desperate would take it. The Famine Commission of 1880 said so, in the government's own words.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the strongest evidence in the argument about whether British rule impoverished India, and it is also where the Indian nationalist economic critique was born.

evidence.author: Mike Davis
evidence.work: Late Victorian Holocausts: El Nino Famines and the Making of the Third World
evidence.supports: The famine, the export data and the relief policy; his mortality estimates are at the high end and are disputed.

evidence.author: Tirthankar Roy
evidence.work: The Economic History of India 1857-1947
evidence.supports: The counter-argument that climate and market integration, not policy alone, drove famine mortality.

contested.note: The death toll and the weight of blame are both disputed. Mike Davis argues that policy turned drought into mass death; Tirthankar Roy argues that the causes were largely climatic and that the colonial state's capacity was simply small. The export figures and the ration levels are not in dispute.

events.title: The Indian National Congress is founded
events.summary: Seventy-two delegates, mostly lawyers, journalists and teachers, met in Bombay at the suggestion of a retired British civil servant, Allan Octavian Hume, to ask for more Indian representation in government. They did not ask for independence.
events.significance: The organisation that would demand and win independence began as a loyal petitioning body of professionals. Its journey from asking for civil service exams in India to demanding that Britain quit is the political history of the Raj in one institution.

places.name: Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay
places.note: Where the first session met in December 1885.

people.name: Allan Octavian Hume
people.role: retired Indian Civil Service officer who convened the first meeting

people.name: Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee
people.role: Calcutta barrister and first president of the Congress

people.name: Dadabhai Naoroji
people.role: president three times and, in 1892, the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons, for Finsbury Central

people.name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
people.role: led the radical wing that broke with the moderates at Surat in 1907 and demanded self-rule as a right

pedagogy.hook: The party that ended British rule in India was set up with the encouragement of a retired British civil servant, and spent its first twenty years writing polite petitions.

misconception.belief: Colonies wanted independence and Britain eventually granted it.
misconception.correction: Congress asked for representation for two decades and was refused. Naoroji sat in the British Parliament and was called a 'black man' by the Prime Minister who lost the seat to him. The demand hardened because the requests failed: swaraj became the goal in 1906, and full independence only in 1929, forty-four years after the first meeting.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the best single case study of how anti-colonial politics actually developed: not a sudden uprising, but decades of refused requests turning into a mass movement.

evidence.author: Judith M. Brown
evidence.work: Modern India: The Origins of an Asian Democracy
evidence.supports: The founding of Congress and the development of nationalist politics.

events.title: The famines of 1896-1902
events.summary: Two great droughts, in 1896-97 and 1899-1900, hit central India, the Deccan and Rajputana. The Famine Codes were applied and relief works employed millions, but mortality in the Central Provinces and the princely states was still catastrophic.
events.significance: These famines killed millions under a system explicitly designed after 1880 to prevent that. They discredited the claim that British administration protected India from starvation, and helped turn moderate nationalism into something angrier.

places.name: Nagpur
places.note: Capital of the Central Provinces, the worst-hit province in 1899-1900.

people.name: George Curzon
people.role: Viceroy during the 1899-1900 famine, who insisted relief be given but warned against 'excessive' generosity

people.name: Romesh Chunder Dutt
people.role: former ICS officer whose open letters to Curzon in 1900 blamed the land revenue system for the scale of the deaths

toll.note: Estimates for the two famines together vary enormously depending on whether the princely states are included, how the baseline is set, and whether epidemic deaths are counted. Official Indian government figures were far lower than modern reconstructions.
toll.source: Government of India famine returns for the low figures; the excess-death reconstructions in Mike Davis, Late Victorian Holocausts (2001), for the high ones.

pedagogy.hook: India built famine relief rules in 1880 to make sure 1877 could not happen again, and in 1900 it happened again.

misconception.belief: Once Britain introduced modern administration, mass deaths from famine stopped.
misconception.correction: The Famine Codes were real, the relief works employed over four million people at their peak, and millions still died. Relief was tied to hard labour, arrived late in the princely states, and did not touch the underlying problem: cultivators with no reserves, a fixed cash revenue demand, and no way to buy food when prices tripled.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the test of whether colonial administration worked on its own terms, and the answer, on the government's own numbers, is that it did not.

evidence.author: Tirthankar Roy
evidence.work: Natural Disasters and Indian History
evidence.supports: The famine codes, the relief system and the debate over mortality.

evidence.author: Mike Davis
evidence.work: Late Victorian Holocausts: El Nino Famines and the Making of the Third World
evidence.supports: The 1899-1900 famine and its political handling; his figures are contested.

contested.note: Mortality estimates for 1896-1902 range from about one to nine million and depend on decisions about baselines, epidemic deaths and whether princely-state deaths are counted. Confidence is marked low because the number itself is genuinely unsettled.

events.title: The first partition of Bengal
events.summary: Curzon split Bengal, a province of 78 million, into a Hindu-majority west and a Muslim-majority east, saying it was for administrative efficiency. Bengalis read it as an attempt to break their politics, and answered with the swadeshi boycott of British goods.
events.significance: The first mass nationalist campaign in India: boycotts, bonfires of Manchester cloth, student strikes and the beginnings of revolutionary violence. Britain reversed the partition in 1911 and moved the capital to Delhi, and the reversal taught nationalists that pressure worked.

places.name: Calcutta
places.note: Where the swadeshi movement was organised and where the capital was until 1911.

places.name: Dacca
places.note: Capital of the new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam, and where the Muslim League was founded in 1906.

people.name: George Curzon
