people.role: Viceroy who ordered the partition and denied it was political

people.name: Surendranath Banerjee
people.role: led the moderate campaign against the partition and the swadeshi boycott

people.name: Rabindranath Tagore
people.role: wrote the song Amar Sonar Bangla for the anti-partition movement; it is now the national anthem of Bangladesh

people.name: Nawab Salimullah of Dacca
people.role: supported the partition as good for eastern Bengal's Muslims and helped found the All-India Muslim League in 1906

pedagogy.hook: The national anthem of Bangladesh was written in 1905 to protest against a British plan to divide Bengal.

misconception.belief: British administrators drew lines for practical reasons and were surprised when people objected.
misconception.correction: Curzon's own officials wrote that the partition would weaken Bengali political agitation by splitting it. The Home Secretary of the Bengal government, Herbert Risley, put it in a minute in 1904: dividing Bengal would divide its opposition. Efficiency was the public reason; the private one was written down.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is where mass politics starts in India, where the Muslim League is founded, and where the idea of dividing Bengal along religious lines is first put on paper, forty-two years before it happened for good.

evidence.author: Sumit Sarkar
evidence.work: The Swadeshi Movement in Bengal 1903-1908
evidence.supports: The partition, the boycott movement and its social limits.

events.title: The Delhi Durbar and the move of the capital
events.summary: George V, the only reigning British monarch ever to visit India, announced at a durbar attended by around 100,000 people that the partition of Bengal was cancelled and the capital would move from Calcutta to Delhi.
events.significance: Two concessions in one speech: a nationalist campaign had forced the reversal of a Viceroy's decision, and the government moved away from Calcutta, the centre of that campaign, to build a new imperial capital on the site of Mughal Delhi.

places.name: Coronation Park, Delhi
places.note: Site of the 1911 durbar; the statues of British officials moved there after 1947 still stand.

places.name: New Delhi
places.note: Designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker from 1912 and inaugurated in 1931, sixteen years before independence.

people.name: George V
people.role: the only British monarch to visit India as reigning king-emperor

people.name: Edwin Lutyens
people.role: architect of the new imperial capital, completed sixteen years before the empire left it

people.name: Charles Hardinge
people.role: Viceroy who proposed the move and survived a bomb thrown at him entering Delhi in 1912

pedagogy.hook: Britain finished building its magnificent new capital at New Delhi in 1931 and handed it over to independent India sixteen years later.

misconception.belief: Imperial rulers in 1911 knew their empire was temporary.
misconception.correction: They were building for centuries. Lutyens's Delhi was laid out on an imperial scale with a viceroy's palace bigger than Versailles, begun in 1912 and opened in 1931. The Government of India Act 1935, which conceded provincial autonomy, was passed four years later, and the whole thing was Indian twelve years after that.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the best physical evidence of imperial confidence and its limits: the buildings that were meant to say permanence now house the government that replaced it.

evidence.author: Robert Grant Irving
evidence.work: Indian Summer: Lutyens, Baker, and Imperial Delhi
evidence.supports: The durbar, the decision to move the capital and the building of New Delhi.

events.title: India in the First World War
events.summary: About 1.4 million Indians served, in France, Mesopotamia, East Africa, Gallipoli and Palestine. Roughly 74,000 died. India also paid a war contribution of 100 million pounds and supplied food, animals and munitions.
events.significance: Indians expected political reward for the largest voluntary war effort in the empire, and got the Rowlatt Acts and Amritsar instead. The gap between the contribution and the return radicalised Indian politics more than any single British decision.

places.name: Neuve-Chapelle
places.note: Where the Indian Corps led the attack in March 1915; the memorial there names 4,742 Indian soldiers with no known grave.

places.name: Kut-al-Amara
places.note: Where an Indian Army division surrendered after a 147-day siege in April 1916.

people.name: Khudadad Khan
people.role: machine gunner from Punjab, the first Indian awarded the Victoria Cross, at Hollebeke in October 1914

people.name: Ganga Singh
people.role: Maharaja of Bikaner, who commanded his own camel corps in France and signed the Treaty of Versailles for India

people.name: Michael O'Dwyer
people.role: Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab who drove recruitment hard, and who backed the Amritsar shootings in 1919

toll.note: Commonwealth War Graves Commission and Indian Army figures give roughly 62,000 to 74,000 Indian dead depending on whether deaths from disease and after discharge are included. About 67,000 were wounded.

pedagogy.hook: About 1.4 million Indians served in the First World War, and India paid Britain 100 million pounds towards the cost of it.

misconception.belief: The World Wars were European wars that the empire watched.
misconception.correction: Indian troops were in France within six weeks of the declaration and held a section of the line at Ypres in 1914 before British divisions arrived. Indian, African and Caribbean soldiers fought in Mesopotamia, East Africa, Palestine and Gallipoli. India paid for it too, out of taxes raised in a country with no vote on the decision.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The war made Indian nationalism a mass movement: the men who came home, and the families of those who did not, had been promised something, and in 1919 they were given the Rowlatt Acts.

evidence.author: David Omissi
evidence.work: Indian Voices of the Great War: Soldiers' Letters 1914-18
evidence.supports: The experience of Indian soldiers, from their own censored letters.

evidence.author: Santanu Das
evidence.work: India, Empire and First World War Culture
evidence.supports: The scale of the Indian war effort and its cultural and political consequences.

events.title: Jallianwala Bagh
events.summary: Troops under Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer fired for about ten minutes into a crowd of several thousand penned in a walled garden in Amritsar with almost no exits. The official Hunter Commission counted 379 dead and about 1,200 wounded; Indian estimates were far higher.
events.significance: It destroyed the case for constitutional loyalty. Gandhi returned his war medals, Tagore renounced his knighthood, and the non-cooperation movement of 1920 followed directly. The Hunter Committee reported; the Army Council then took Dyer's command from him and gave him no further employment. A public subscription in Britain raised over 26,000 pounds in his honour.

places.name: Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar
places.note: A walled enclosure of about six acres with five narrow exits, one of which Dyer blocked with his troops.

people.name: Reginald Dyer
people.role: ordered the firing, said afterwards he would have used machine guns if the armoured cars had fitted through the entrance

people.name: Michael O'Dwyer
people.role: Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab who approved Dyer's action and imposed martial law; shot dead in London in 1940 by Udham Singh

people.name: Udham Singh
people.role: survivor of the massacre who killed O'Dwyer at Caxton Hall in March 1940 and was hanged

people.name: Rabindranath Tagore
people.role: renounced his knighthood in protest on 31 May 1919

people.name: Saifuddin Kitchlew
people.role: Amritsar Congress leader whose arrest triggered the protests; later awarded the Lenin Peace Prize

toll.note: The Hunter Commission accepted 379 dead. The Indian National Congress inquiry put it at over 1,000, and a 1919 count by the Amritsar civil authorities listed 501 names. The garden was walled and the exits blocked; nobody could leave to be counted.
toll.source: The Hunter Commission report (1920) for 379; the Indian National Congress inquiry (1920) for over 1,000; the Amritsar civil authorities' list of 501 names, compiled in 1919.

pedagogy.hook: After the Amritsar shootings, a British newspaper opened a fund for General Dyer and raised over 26,000 pounds, roughly a million in today's money.

misconception.belief: Amritsar was a tragic incident in which protesters lost their lives.
misconception.correction: It was a decision. Dyer marched troops into a walled enclosure, blocked the main exit, gave no warning, and ordered 1,650 rounds fired into a crowd until the ammunition ran low. He told the Hunter Commission he intended to produce a moral effect throughout the Punjab. The words 'incident' and 'lost their lives' hide who did what.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The reaction in Britain, where Dyer was celebrated by a large section of opinion, did more damage to the Raj's legitimacy in India than the shooting itself.

evidence.author: Kim A. Wagner
evidence.work: Amritsar 1919: An Empire of Fear and the Making of a Massacre
evidence.supports: The massacre, the martial law regime that followed and the British reaction.

contested.note: The death toll is disputed: 379 official, 501 named by the Amritsar authorities, over 1,000 claimed by the Congress inquiry. The official figure came from a commission with limited access and no power to compel evidence.

events.title: The Rowlatt Acts and the Act of 1919
events.summary: In March 1919 the Rowlatt Act extended wartime detention without trial into peacetime, against the votes of every elected Indian member. In December the Government of India Act introduced dyarchy: Indian ministers got education and health, the Governor kept police, revenue and land.
events.significance: The two acts together are the empire's answer to India's war effort: repression first, then a limited share of the powers that did not matter. About 3% of adults got a vote, and Gandhi's first all-India campaign began between the two.

places.name: Imperial Legislative Council, Delhi
places.note: Where every elected Indian member voted against the Rowlatt Bill and it passed anyway.

people.name: Edwin Montagu
people.role: Secretary of State for India whose 1917 declaration promised the gradual development of self-governing institutions

people.name: Frederic Thesiger, 1st Viscount Chelmsford
people.role: Viceroy, co-author of the reforms and of the Rowlatt legislation

people.name: Mohandas Gandhi
people.role: called a nationwide hartal against the Rowlatt Act in April 1919, his first all-India campaign

people.name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
people.role: resigned from the Imperial Legislative Council in protest at the Rowlatt Act

pedagogy.hook: Every elected Indian member of the legislature voted against the Rowlatt Act, and it passed anyway; that is what the pre-1919 constitution was for.

misconception.belief: Reform and repression were separate British policies pursued by different governments.
misconception.correction: They were the same policy in the same year. The Rowlatt Act of March 1919 and the reform act of December 1919 were passed nine months apart by the same administration. Concede the form, keep the substance, and legislate the power to detain anyone who does not accept the deal.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest single illustration of how the Raj managed nationalism, and of why Gandhi concluded that cooperation with it was pointless.

evidence.author: Judith M. Brown
evidence.work: Gandhi's Rise to Power: Indian Politics 1915-1922
evidence.supports: The Rowlatt agitation, the reforms and Gandhi's emergence as a national leader.

events.title: Non-cooperation and Khilafat
events.summary: Congress under Gandhi voted to withdraw from British schools, courts, councils and titles, and allied with the Khilafat movement of Indian Muslims defending the Ottoman caliphate. Millions took part. Gandhi called it off after a crowd burned twenty-two policemen to death at Chauri Chaura.
events.significance: The first mass campaign of the independence movement and the high point of Hindu-Muslim political alliance. Its sudden cancellation split Congress, disillusioned the Khilafat leaders, and set the pattern for every campaign that followed.

places.name: Chauri Chaura
places.note: Where a crowd burned a police station on 4 February 1922, killing twenty-two policemen, after police fired on a procession.

places.name: Nagpur
places.note: Where the Congress session of December 1920 adopted the non-cooperation programme.

people.name: Mohandas Gandhi
people.role: designed and led the campaign, then called it off unilaterally after Chauri Chaura and was jailed for six years

people.name: Muhammad Ali Jauhar
people.role: with his brother Shaukat, led the Khilafat movement and brought hundreds of thousands of Muslims into the campaign

people.name: Motilal Nehru
people.role: gave up a large legal practice to join the boycott of the courts

people.name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
people.role: opposed non-cooperation as unconstitutional and left Congress over it in 1920

toll.note: Includes police firings across India and the Moplah rebellion in Malabar in 1921, which grew out of the Khilafat agitation and in which perhaps 2,300 rebels and an unknown number of civilians died. Figures come from official reports.

pedagogy.hook: Gandhi called off the biggest protest movement India had ever seen because a crowd in one small town killed twenty-two policemen.

misconception.belief: Non-violent resistance means protest that has no cost and breaks no rules.
misconception.correction: Non-cooperation meant lawyers leaving their practices, students leaving universities, officials resigning and thousands going to prison. Gandhi's discipline was strict enough that he ended the campaign at its peak rather than let it turn violent, a decision Subhas Bose and many in Congress never forgave.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the moment Indian nationalism becomes a mass movement rather than a professional one, and the moment its central strategic argument, discipline against escalation, is set.

evidence.author: Shahid Amin
evidence.work: Event, Metaphor, Memory: Chauri Chaura 1922-1992
evidence.supports: Chauri Chaura, its trial and its place in nationalist memory.

events.title: The Salt March and civil disobedience
events.summary: Gandhi walked 385 km from Ahmedabad to Dandi with 78 companions and picked up a lump of natural salt, breaking the government's salt monopoly. Civil disobedience spread nationwide; about 60,000 people were jailed, and at Dharasana marchers were beaten down in rows without raising a hand.
events.significance: It turned a tax on a household necessity into an argument the world could follow, and it put Indian independence on front pages from New York to Berlin. It also forced Britain to the Round Table Conferences and the Gandhi-Irwin pact.

places.name: Dandi
places.note: The coastal village where Gandhi broke the salt law on 6 April 1930.

places.name: Dharasana Salt Works
places.note: Where about 2,500 volunteers walked into police lathis in rows in May 1930; Webb Miller's report went round the world.

places.name: Peshawar
places.note: Where the Khudai Khidmatgar joined the campaign and were fired on at Qissa Khwani bazaar in April 1930.

people.name: Mohandas Gandhi
people.role: led the march and chose salt as the target because everyone, rich and poor, had to buy it

people.name: Sarojini Naidu
people.role: led the Dharasana raid after Gandhi's arrest; poet and later the first woman governor of an Indian province

people.name: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
people.role: brought the Khudai Khidmatgar into the campaign on the North-West Frontier

people.name: Edward Wood, Lord Irwin
people.role: Viceroy who jailed 60,000 people and then negotiated with Gandhi as an equal in 1931, which Churchill called nauseating

toll.note: Deaths in police firings across India during the civil disobedience campaign of 1930-31, from official returns which nationalists said undercounted. About 60,000 to 90,000 people were imprisoned.

pedagogy.hook: Gandhi chose salt because the tax on it was the one thing every Indian, however poor, had to pay to a government they had not elected.

misconception.belief: Gandhi's methods were symbolic gestures that did not really threaten British power.
misconception.correction: The salt campaign put 60,000 people in prison, cost the government its revenue monopoly's authority, and made the Viceroy negotiate with a man he had just jailed. Its real weapon was the photograph: Webb Miller's account of Dharasana, where volunteers were clubbed down in silent rows, was printed in more than a thousand newspapers.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows how a well-chosen symbol converts a moral argument into political pressure, and it is the direct model for later civil rights movements from Montgomery to Johannesburg.

evidence.author: Judith M. Brown
evidence.work: Gandhi: Prisoner of Hope
evidence.supports: The salt campaign, its organisation and its political effect.

events.title: The Government of India Act 1935
events.summary: The longest Act ever passed by Parliament at that time gave elected provincial governments real power, extended the vote to about 35 million people, roughly a sixth of adults, and separated Burma and Aden from India. The proposed all-India federation never came into being.
events.significance: Congress won eight of eleven provinces in 1937 and governed them; the Muslim League did badly and drew the conclusion that in a united India it would always be a permanent minority. Much of the Act survives as the framework of the Indian and Pakistani constitutions.

places.name: Westminster
places.note: Where the bill took eighteen months and 4,000 speeches to pass, against Churchill's opposition.

people.name: Samuel Hoare
people.role: Secretary of State for India who steered the Act through against fierce Conservative resistance

people.name: Winston Churchill
people.role: led the parliamentary campaign against the Act, arguing that Indians were unfit to govern themselves

people.name: B. R. Ambedkar
people.role: negotiated the Poona Pact of 1932 with Gandhi over separate electorates for Dalits, which shaped the Act's electoral scheme

people.name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
people.role: returned from London in 1935 to rebuild the Muslim League after its poor showing under the new franchise

pedagogy.hook: The 1935 Act gave Indians the vote in numbers Britain had never allowed before, and the Muslim League's defeat in the elections it produced is one reason Pakistan exists.

misconception.belief: Britain gradually handed power to Indians as they became ready for it.
misconception.correction: The Act was passed to contain the civil disobedience movement, not to reward it, and its centrepiece, a federation including the princely states, was designed to give the princes a permanent conservative block in the centre. That federation never happened because the princes refused. The provincial elections it did produce hardened the split that led to partition.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the constitutional bridge between the Raj and the two states that replaced it: most of independent India's and Pakistan's early constitutional machinery is lifted from it.

evidence.author: Ayesha Jalal
evidence.work: The Sole Spokesman: Jinnah, the Muslim League and the Demand for Pakistan
evidence.supports: The effect of the 1937 elections on Muslim League strategy.

events.title: Burma leaves India without leaving the empire
events.summary: Under the Government of Burma Act 1935, Burma stopped being a province of British India and became a separate colony with its own Governor, cabinet and legislature. Aden was detached from India on the same day.
events.significance: A territory changed its place in the empire without changing hands. It shows that 'British' was an administrative category as much as a political one, and it left Burma outside the Indian independence negotiations a decade later.

places.name: Rangoon
places.note: Capital of the new colony from 1 April 1937.

people.name: Ba Maw
people.role: first Premier of separated Burma; later head of the Japanese-sponsored government from 1943

people.name: U Saw
people.role: Premier 1940-42, arrested by the British for contacting the Japanese, and hanged in 1948 for Aung San's murder

pedagogy.hook: On 1 April 1937 Burma stopped being part of India and stayed just as British as before.

misconception.belief: A place either was or was not part of the British Empire, and the map colour tells you which.
misconception.correction: Burma was British before 1937 and after it; only its filing changed. Aden moved the same day from the Government of India to the Colonial Office. Territories moved between administrations, statuses and even continents on the empire's own organisation charts, which is why a single colour on a map hides more than it shows.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the cleanest example in the atlas of an internal reorganisation that looks like a border change and is not, and it explains why Burma negotiated its independence separately in 1947.

evidence.author: Michael W. Charney
evidence.work: A History of Modern Burma
evidence.supports: The separation of 1937 and Burmese nationalist reactions to it.

events.title: Quit India
events.summary: Congress demanded immediate British withdrawal and Gandhi told Indians to 'do or die'. The entire leadership was arrested within twelve hours. The rising that followed cut railways and telegraphs across eastern India and was put down with troops, mass arrests and aerial strafing.
events.significance: The last great campaign before independence, and the most violently suppressed: over 90,000 arrested and around a thousand killed by official count. It also removed Congress from politics for three years, which left the field to the Muslim League.

places.name: Gowalia Tank, Bombay
places.note: Where the Quit India resolution was passed on 8 August 1942.

places.name: Ballia
places.note: One of several districts where rebels set up short-lived independent administrations in August 1942.

people.name: Mohandas Gandhi
people.role: moved the resolution and was interned at the Aga Khan Palace in Poona for twenty-one months

people.name: Aruna Asaf Ali
people.role: raised the Congress flag at Gowalia Tank after the arrests and led the underground movement

people.name: Jayaprakash Narayan
people.role: escaped from Hazaribagh jail and organised armed underground resistance

people.name: Archibald Wavell
people.role: Commander-in-Chief, then Viceroy from October 1943; used over fifty battalions against the rising

people.name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
people.role: opposed Quit India and used the three years of Congress imprisonment to build the Muslim League's mass base

toll.note: Official figures gave about 1,060 killed and 3,200 injured in police and military firing; Congress claimed far higher. Over 90,000 were arrested and detained without trial.

pedagogy.hook: Britain arrested the entire leadership of India's largest political party within twelve hours of the Quit India resolution, and kept them in jail for three years.

misconception.belief: Independence was granted because Britain became convinced it was the right thing to do.
misconception.correction: In 1942 Britain jailed 90,000 people, used aircraft against crowds, and held the Congress leadership until 1945 to keep India in the war. Five years later it left, because it was bankrupt, because the 1946 naval mutiny showed the Indian armed forces could not be relied on, and because holding India would have cost more than Britain had.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Quit India is the last hinge before partition: it removed Congress from politics at exactly the moment the Muslim League was building the support that made Pakistan possible.

evidence.author: Yasmin Khan
evidence.work: The Raj at War: A People's History of India's Second World War
evidence.supports: The suppression of Quit India and the wartime state in India.

events.title: The Bengal famine of 1943
events.summary: Between two and three million people died in Bengal. The rice harvest had been damaged and Burma's exports were cut off by the Japanese, but grain kept moving out of the province, boats and stocks were destroyed under a wartime denial policy, and London refused most of the shipping the Viceroy asked for.
events.significance: The last great famine in British India, and the one with the fullest documentation of the decisions behind it. Amartya Sen's analysis of it changed how economists understand famine everywhere: the deaths came from collapsing entitlements, not an absolute shortage of food.

places.name: Calcutta
places.note: Kept supplied by priority rationing for war industry while the countryside starved and destitute villagers died in its streets.

places.name: Midnapore
places.note: Where the boat denial policy destroyed some 46,000 country boats used for fishing and moving rice.

people.name: Winston Churchill
people.role: Prime Minister; his War Cabinet repeatedly refused or reduced shipping for Indian grain imports in 1943

people.name: Archibald Wavell
people.role: Viceroy from October 1943, who used the army to distribute food and told London the famine was a stain on its record

people.name: Leo Amery
people.role: Secretary of State for India, who pressed the War Cabinet for grain shipments and was overruled

people.name: Amartya Sen
people.role: economist, nine years old in Bengal in 1943; his 1981 analysis of the famine won him the Nobel Prize

people.name: Chittaprosad Bhattacharya
people.role: artist whose drawings of the famine were published in 1943 and then seized and burned by the government

toll.note: The Famine Inquiry Commission of 1945 said 1.5 million; demographic reconstructions since have given between 2.1 and 3 million, depending on the period counted and whether later epidemic deaths are included.
toll.source: The Famine Inquiry Commission's Report on Bengal (1945) for 1.5 million; Amartya Sen, Poverty and Famines (1981), and the demographic reconstructions by Tim Dyson and Arup Maharatna for the 2.1 to 3 million range.

pedagogy.hook: Bengal produced enough rice in 1943 to feed itself; between two and three million people died anyway.

misconception.belief: A terrible famine struck Bengal in 1943 and killed millions.
misconception.correction: The word 'struck' hides the decisions. The 1942 harvest was poor and Burmese imports had stopped, but Bengal's total food availability in 1943 was not much below normal. Prices tripled, wages did not, and the people who died were those who could no longer buy. Grain left the province, boats were destroyed by policy, and the War Cabinet refused most of the shipping requested.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the best-documented famine in the empire's history and the one where responsibility can be traced to named decisions in recorded meetings, which is why it dominates the argument about British rule.

evidence.author: Amartya Sen
evidence.work: Poverty and Famines: An Essay on Entitlement and Deprivation
evidence.supports: The entitlement analysis of the 1943 famine and the food availability data.

evidence.author: Janam Mukherjee
evidence.work: Hungry Bengal: War, Famine and the End of Empire
evidence.supports: The denial policies, the wartime administration and the course of the famine.

contested.note: The death toll ranges from the 1945 commission's 1.5 million to about 3 million in later work, depending on the window counted. Responsibility is also argued: some historians stress Churchill's War Cabinet decisions, others provincial mismanagement, hoarding and the wartime emergency.

events.title: Bose, the INA and the Red Fort trials
events.summary: Subhas Chandra Bose escaped house arrest, reached Germany and then Japan by submarine, and led an Indian National Army of prisoners of war and Malayan Indians against the British in Burma. Its officers were tried at the Red Fort in 1945, and the trials caused mutinies.
events.significance: The INA lost militarily and won politically. Its trials made British officers realise that the Indian Army, the instrument that had held India for two centuries, could no longer be relied on to hold it against Indians.

places.name: Red Fort, Delhi
places.note: Where three INA officers were tried in November 1945, deliberately staged in the Mughal palace.

places.name: Port Blair
places.note: Where Bose raised the flag of Azad Hind on 30 December 1943.

places.name: Imphal
places.note: Where the Japanese and INA advance into India was stopped in 1944.

people.name: Subhas Chandra Bose
people.role: Congress president in 1938-39, escaped India in 1941 and led the INA and the Provisional Government of Azad Hind; died in an air crash in Taiwan in August 1945

people.name: Lakshmi Sahgal
people.role: doctor who commanded the INA's Rani of Jhansi Regiment, one of the first all-female combat units in Asia

people.name: Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Sahgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon
people.role: the three officers, a Muslim, a Hindu and a Sikh, tried together at the Red Fort in a case that united Indian opinion

people.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
people.role: put on his barrister's robes for the first time in twenty-five years to help defend the INA officers

people.name: Claude Auchinleck
people.role: Commander-in-Chief who commuted the sentences, warning London that the Indian Army's loyalty was at stake

toll.note: Estimated INA deaths from combat, disease and starvation in the Burma campaign, chiefly in the 1944 retreat from Imphal. Records were destroyed and the figures are approximate.

pedagogy.hook: In February 1946 sailors of the Royal Indian Navy mutinied in Bombay harbour, and within three weeks Britain announced a Cabinet Mission to negotiate independence.

misconception.belief: Indian independence was won entirely by non-violent protest.
misconception.correction: Gandhi's movements were decisive, but so was the collapse of confidence in the army and navy. The Red Fort trials produced riots in Calcutta and Bombay, then the naval mutiny of February 1946, in which 20,000 sailors on 78 ships struck. Wavell told London the Indian services could no longer be relied on against Indians, and that was the end of the argument for staying.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the strongest evidence for the argument that Britain left because holding India had become impossible, not because it chose to go.

evidence.author: Sugata Bose
evidence.work: His Majesty's Opponent: Subhas Chandra Bose and India's Struggle Against Empire
evidence.supports: Bose's career, the INA and the Provisional Government of Azad Hind.

evidence.author: Yasmin Khan
evidence.work: The Raj at War: A People's History of India's Second World War
evidence.supports: The war in India, the INA trials and the 1946 mutinies.

contested.note: How much the INA and the 1946 mutinies mattered to the timing of independence is disputed: some historians make them decisive, others treat British financial exhaustion and the 1945 Labour government's priorities as the main causes. Bose's death in August 1945 is also the subject of long-running conspiracy claims that three official inquiries have rejected.

events.title: Direct Action Day and the Cabinet Mission
events.summary: The Cabinet Mission proposed a loose federation with grouped provinces instead of partition. Both parties accepted and then reinterpreted it. Jinnah called a Direct Action Day for 16 August 1946; about 4,000 people died in Calcutta in four days, and the killing spread to Noakhali and Bihar.
events.significance: The last chance to avoid partition failed on a disagreement about whether provinces could opt out of their groups. After Calcutta, the argument was no longer about constitutions: Congress and the League each now believed the other would not protect their people.

places.name: Calcutta
places.note: Where about 4,000 people were killed between 16 and 19 August 1946.

places.name: Noakhali
places.note: Where attacks on Hindus in October 1946 brought Gandhi to walk the district village by village for four months.

places.name: Simla
places.note: Where the Cabinet Mission's conference with Congress and League leaders broke down in May 1946.

people.name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
people.role: called Direct Action Day after concluding that constitutional negotiation had failed

people.name: H. S. Suhrawardy
people.role: Muslim League Premier of Bengal, in office in Calcutta during the killings; later worked with Gandhi to stop them

people.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
people.role: whose July 1946 statement that Congress was not bound by the grouping scheme gave Jinnah his reason to withdraw

people.name: Mohandas Gandhi
people.role: walked barefoot through Noakhali from November 1946 to March 1947 to stop the killing, village by village

people.name: Archibald Wavell
people.role: Viceroy who convened the mission and was replaced by Mountbatten in March 1947 for being too pessimistic

toll.note: About 4,000 died in Calcutta in four days, with roughly 100,000 left homeless. The Noakhali and Bihar killings that followed added several thousand more; the Bihar figure is especially uncertain.

pedagogy.hook: The plan that might have kept India whole failed over a single question: whether a province could leave the group it had been put in.

misconception.belief: Partition was inevitable because Hindus and Muslims could never live in one state.
misconception.correction: In May 1946 both Congress and the Muslim League accepted a plan for one federal India with grouped provinces. It collapsed within weeks over a technical disagreement about opting out, and Nehru's press conference in July made Jinnah conclude the guarantees were worthless. Partition became likely in the summer of 1946, not in some ancient past.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows partition as a political failure with a date and a cause, which is a far more useful thing for a student to be able to explain than 'ancient hatreds'.

evidence.author: Ayesha Jalal
evidence.work: The Sole Spokesman: Jinnah, the Muslim League and the Demand for Pakistan
evidence.supports: The Cabinet Mission negotiations and Jinnah's strategy.

evidence.author: Yasmin Khan
evidence.work: The Great Partition: The Making of India and Pakistan
evidence.supports: Direct Action Day, the Calcutta killings and their political effect.

contested.note: Responsibility for the collapse of the Cabinet Mission plan is one of the sharpest disputes in South Asian history, and Pakistani and Indian textbooks give opposite answers about whether Nehru's July statement or Jinnah's Direct Action call was the decisive step.

events.title: Partition and independence
events.summary: Mountbatten arrived in March 1947, brought the transfer forward from June 1948 to August 1947, and left in seventy-three days. Cyril Radcliffe drew the border in about five weeks and it was published on 17 August, two days after the countries it divided came into being.
events.significance: The largest forced migration in recorded history: between 12 and 18 million people crossed the new lines, and hundreds of thousands were killed. It also removed about three quarters of the empire's population in a single day, and almost none of its territory.

places.name: Lahore
places.note: Expected by many to go to India; awarded to Pakistan.

places.name: Amritsar
places.note: Forty kilometres from Lahore, on the Indian side; the two cities emptied of each other's people.

places.name: New Delhi
places.note: Where Radcliffe worked from maps and 1941 census returns in a bungalow, and where Nehru made the 'tryst with destiny' speech at midnight.

people.name: Cyril Radcliffe
people.role: chairman of both boundary commissions; had never been east of Suez, drew the line in about five weeks and burned his papers

people.name: Louis Mountbatten
people.role: last Viceroy; brought the date forward by ten months and became independent India's first Governor-General

people.name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
people.role: first Governor-General of Pakistan; died thirteen months later

people.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
people.role: first Prime Minister of India

people.name: Mohandas Gandhi
people.role: spent independence day fasting in Calcutta; assassinated on 30 January 1948 by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for partition

people.name: Vallabhbhai Patel
people.role: brought over 500 princely states into India within two years

toll.note: No authority was counting. The lower death figure is the contemporary official estimate, the higher the outer edge of scholarly estimates; most historians work with several hundred thousand to about a million. Tens of thousands of women were abducted, and both states later organised their forcible recovery.
toll.source: Contemporary official estimates for the low figure; the range in Yasmin Khan, The Great Partition (2007), and Ian Talbot and Gurharpal Singh, The Partition of India (2009). No authority counted at the time.

pedagogy.hook: The border between India and Pakistan was published two days after the two countries existed, so millions of people spent independence day not knowing which country they were in.

misconception.belief: Partition was a tragic event in which violence broke out between communities.
misconception.correction: Name the process. A British lawyer with no knowledge of India drew a line in five weeks using out-of-date census maps. The date was brought forward by ten months. The Punjab Boundary Force of 50,000 was too small and was disbanded on 1 September. Between ten and twenty million people fled. 'Violence broke out' describes weather, not decisions.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Partition made two, then three, countries; it caused four wars; it produced two nuclear arsenals; and the border it drew is still the reason Kashmir is the most militarised place on earth.

evidence.author: Yasmin Khan
evidence.work: The Great Partition: The Making of India and Pakistan
evidence.supports: The speed of the transfer, the violence and the displacement figures.

evidence.author: Ian Talbot and Gurharpal Singh
evidence.work: The Partition of India
evidence.supports: The boundary commissions, the migration and the historiographical debate over responsibility.

evidence.author: Urvashi Butalia
evidence.work: The Other Side of Silence: Voices from the Partition of India
evidence.supports: The experience of partition, especially of women, from oral testimony.

contested.note: Responsibility is genuinely disputed between Congress intransigence, Jinnah's demand and a British departure so rushed that no orderly transfer was possible. The death toll is disputed because no one counted, and the displacement range reflects different definitions of who was a refugee.

events.title: The accession of the princely states
events.summary: British paramountcy over 565 princely states simply lapsed at independence, leaving each ruler legally free. Almost all acceded to India or Pakistan within weeks. Three did not: Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir, and each was settled by force or the threat of it.
events.significance: The states covered two fifths of India and a quarter of its people. Their absorption in two years is why the map of India looks continuous today, and the three that resisted produced the Kashmir dispute, Operation Polo and a plebiscite in Junagadh.

places.name: Junagadh
places.note: Acceded to Pakistan on 15 September 1947; India took it over on 9 November and held a plebiscite in February 1948.

places.name: Hyderabad
places.note: Refused to accede; invaded by India on 13 September 1948.

places.name: Srinagar
places.note: Where Indian troops landed on 27 October 1947 after the maharaja signed the accession.

people.name: Vallabhbhai Patel
people.role: Indian Home Minister who ran the integration, using a mixture of privy purses, threats and, twice, the army

people.name: V. P. Menon
people.role: civil servant who drafted the Instrument of Accession and negotiated with the rulers one by one

people.name: Osman Ali Khan
people.role: Nizam of Hyderabad, who held out for independence for thirteen months

people.name: Hari Singh
people.role: Maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir, who acceded to India in October 1947 under invasion

people.name: Louis Mountbatten
people.role: urged the princes to accede on grounds of geography and warned them that independence was not realistic

pedagogy.hook: On 15 August 1947, 565 Indian rulers became legally independent, and within two years all but a handful had signed their states away.

misconception.belief: India and Pakistan simply inherited British India's borders.
misconception.correction: They inherited the provinces. Two fifths of the subcontinent belonged to princely states whose treaties were with the British Crown, and those treaties lapsed rather than transferring. Every state had to be persuaded, bought or coerced into joining, and the three that refused produced a plebiscite, an invasion and a war that has not ended.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains the shape of modern India and Pakistan, and it is the direct origin of the Kashmir conflict, which is the longest-running dispute on the United Nations agenda.

evidence.author: Barbara N. Ramusack
evidence.work: The Indian Princes and their States
evidence.supports: Paramountcy, its lapse and the process of integration.

evidence.author: V. P. Menon
evidence.work: The Story of the Integration of the Indian States
evidence.supports: The negotiations, from the official who conducted them; a partisan but first-hand account.

contested.note: Whether the accessions of Hyderabad, Junagadh, Kashmir and Kalat were legitimate is argued between Indian, Pakistani and regional nationalist historiographies, and the arguments are still made in courts and at the United Nations.

events.title: Bangladesh, 1971
events.summary: After the Awami League won Pakistan's 1970 election and was refused power, the Pakistan army launched Operation Searchlight in East Pakistan. Nine months of killing, a refugee flight of about ten million into India, and an Indian intervention ended with Bangladesh independent.
events.significance: It completed the unfinished business of 1947. Pakistan had been built on the idea that religion made a nation, and its eastern wing left over language, economics and political representation rather than religion.

places.name: Dhaka
places.note: Where Operation Searchlight began on the night of 25 March 1971 and where Pakistani forces surrendered on 16 December.

places.name: Dhaka University
places.note: Attacked on the first night; academics and students were among the first killed.

people.name: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman
people.role: Awami League leader whose party won the 1970 election and was denied power; arrested on 25 March 1971 and became Bangladesh's first leader

people.name: Yahya Khan
people.role: Pakistan's president who ordered Operation Searchlight

people.name: Indira Gandhi
people.role: Indian Prime Minister who backed the Mukti Bahini and intervened in December 1971

people.name: Archer Blood
people.role: American consul-general in Dhaka whose dissent telegram protested at Washington's silence about the killings

toll.note: Bangladesh's official figure is three million; independent scholarly estimates range from about 300,000 upwards. Between eight and ten million refugees crossed into India. Estimates of women raped range from 200,000 to 400,000. All these figures are contested.

pedagogy.hook: Pakistan was created in 1947 on the argument that religion made a nation; in 1971 its eastern half left because language and votes mattered more.

misconception.belief: The consequences of partition ended in 1947.
misconception.correction: Pakistan's two wings were 1,600 km apart with India between them, and the eastern wing had the larger population and the smaller share of spending, jobs and army posts. Bengali was refused equal status with Urdu in 1948 and students were shot for demanding it in 1952. Bangladesh in 1971 is the second half of 1947.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the last act of the partition, it created the world's eighth most populous country, and it shows how a border drawn for one reason can fail for a different one.

evidence.author: Srinath Raghavan
evidence.work: 1971: A Global History of the Creation of Bangladesh
evidence.supports: The war, the international politics around it and the debate over casualty figures.

evidence.author: Gary J. Bass
evidence.work: The Blood Telegram: Nixon, Kissinger and a Forgotten Genocide
evidence.supports: American policy, the Blood telegram and the scale of the killing.

contested.note: The death toll is among the most disputed of any modern conflict: Bangladesh's official figure of three million against independent estimates that start around 300,000. Whether the killings amounted to genocide is argued in law as well as in history.

events.title: The drain of wealth argument

date.note: The argument runs continuously from Naoroji's first papers in 1867 to present-day work by Utsa Patnaik and Tirthankar Roy; it has no end date because it has not ended.

events.summary: Dadabhai Naoroji argued from 1867 that India was being systematically drained: home charges, pensions, guaranteed railway returns and a trade surplus taken as tribute rather than paid for. Historians have argued about the size of the transfer, and its effects, ever since.
events.significance: It is the founding economic argument of Indian nationalism, and the single most important historiographical dispute about the empire. What students should learn is not a number but why the number is uncertain, and what each side counts.

places.name: India Office, London
places.note: Where the home charges were paid: administration, pensions and debt service, all charged to Indian revenue.

people.name: Dadabhai Naoroji
people.role: made the drain argument from 1867 and put it before the British public as an MP; his Poverty and Un-British Rule in India appeared in 1901

people.name: Romesh Chunder Dutt
people.role: former ICS officer whose Economic History of India of 1902-04 gave the argument its documentary basis

people.name: Utsa Patnaik
people.role: economist whose recent calculations put the total transfer at tens of trillions of dollars in present-day terms

people.name: Tirthankar Roy
people.role: economic historian who argues the drain was small relative to Indian output and that India's stagnation had domestic causes

people.name: Shashi Tharoor
people.role: made the case for reparations in a 2015 Oxford Union speech and in Inglorious Empire, reviving the argument for a mass audience

pedagogy.hook: India's share of world manufacturing output fell from roughly a quarter in 1750 to a few per cent by 1900, while Britain's rose.

misconception.belief: Historians agree about whether the empire made India poorer, and the facts are settled.
misconception.correction: They do not agree, and the disagreement is about method. Naoroji, Dutt and Patnaik count the home charges, guaranteed railway returns and the unpaid export surplus as a transfer. Roy counts total Indian output and argues the transfer was a small share of it. Every one of these counts is a reconstruction with wide error bars. Knowing why the number is uncertain is the skill.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the argument that made Indian nationalism economic rather than merely constitutional, and it is the model for how to handle a contested historical number: name the positions, name the method, and say what would settle it.

evidence.author: Dadabhai Naoroji
evidence.work: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
evidence.supports: The original drain argument in its author's own words.

evidence.author: Tirthankar Roy
evidence.work: The Economic History of India 1857-1947
evidence.supports: The case that the drain was small relative to national income and that stagnation had domestic causes.

evidence.author: Shashi Tharoor
evidence.work: Inglorious Empire: What the British Did to India
evidence.supports: The modern restatement of the extraction case, whose figures are themselves disputed.

contested.note: This record is marked low confidence deliberately: there is no agreed figure for the drain, and the estimates differ by orders of magnitude because they measure different things. The atlas shows the argument, not a verdict.

positions.claim: British rule transferred a large share of India's surplus to Britain and caused deindustrialisation and famine.
positions.heldBy: Naoroji, R. C. Dutt, Utsa Patnaik, Shashi Tharoor

positions.claim: The transfer was small relative to Indian national income, and India's poverty had mainly domestic and agricultural causes.
positions.heldBy: Tirthankar Roy and much recent economic history

events.title: Indian indentured labour
events.summary: Within a year of abolishing slavery, Britain began shipping Indian labourers on five-year indentures to Mauritius, then British Guiana, Trinidad, Natal, Fiji, Ceylon, Malaya and East Africa. About 1.3 to 1.5 million people went under the system before it was abolished in 1917.
events.significance: It replaced enslaved labour with contracted labour on the same plantations, often within a year of emancipation. It also created Indian communities across the empire, from Trinidad to Fiji, and produced the Indian politics that Gandhi first practised in Natal.

places.name: Calcutta emigration depot
places.note: One of the two main embarkation points; the other was Madras.

places.name: Port Louis, Mauritius
places.note: Where the first shipload arrived in 1834; the Aapravasi Ghat there is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

people.name: Mohandas Gandhi
people.role: went to Natal in 1893 as a lawyer for Indian traders and spent twenty-one years there organising indentured and ex-indentured Indians

people.name: Gopal Krishna Gokhale
people.role: moved the resolution in the Imperial Legislative Council in 1912 to abolish indenture

people.name: Totaram Sanadhya
people.role: indentured labourer in Fiji whose 1914 account, My Twenty-One Years in the Fiji Islands, helped end the system

people.name: Kunti
people.role: woman in Fiji whose 1913 account of resisting sexual assault on a plantation was published in India and became a scandal

toll.note: Total Indian emigrants under indenture between 1834 and 1917, from shipping and colonial records. Mortality on the voyages was high in the early decades and fell after the 1860s; the totals do not include the separate Tamil migration to Ceylon and Malaya, which was larger.

pedagogy.hook: Britain abolished slavery in 1834 and started shipping indentured Indians to the same plantations the same year.

misconception.belief: Indenture was just a job with a contract, so it was nothing like slavery.
misconception.correction: It was legally different and that difference was real: a fixed term, a wage, and in principle a return passage. It was also enforced by criminal law, so leaving the plantation was a crime, and recruiters routinely lied about where people were going. Historians describe it as a system between slavery and free labour, which is why the argument about what to call it is worth having carefully.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains why there are Indian-descended majorities or large minorities in Mauritius, Guyana, Trinidad, Fiji and Suriname, and it is where Gandhi learned the politics he later brought to India.

evidence.author: Hugh Tinker
evidence.work: A New System of Slavery: The Export of Indian Labour Overseas, 1830-1920
evidence.supports: The indenture system, its recruitment and its conditions; the title states the argument, which later historians have qualified.

evidence.author: Marina Carter
evidence.work: Servants, Sirdars and Settlers: Indians in Mauritius, 1834-1874
evidence.supports: The Mauritian case and the argument that indentured migrants had more agency than Tinker allowed.

contested.note: Whether indenture is best described as 'a new system of slavery', as Hugh Tinker argued, or as a coerced but not unfree labour migration, as Marina Carter and others argue, is an open dispute. The recruitment abuses and the criminal enforcement are not in dispute.
